Incumbent [[Republican Party (United States)|Republican]] governor [[Sean Parnell]] ran for re-election to a second full term in office, but incumbent [[List of lieutenant governors of Alaska|lieutenant governor]] [[Mead Treadwell]] instead chose to run for the U.S. Senate. [[Partisan primary|Primary elections]] were held on August 19, 2014, to determine party nominees for the office, with separate primaries held for governor and lieutenant governor and the winners running together on the same ticket. Parnell was renominated; his running mate was [[Anchorage, Alaska|Anchorage]] [[List of mayors of Anchorage, Alaska|Mayor]] [[Dan Sullivan (Anchorage mayor)|Dan Sullivan]].Not to be confused with former commissioner of the [[Alaska Department of Natural Resources]] [[Dan Sullivan (U.S. Senator)|Dan Sullivan]] who ran as the Republican nominee in the U.S. Senate election which was held at the same time. The [[Democratic Party (United States)|Democrats]] nominated businessman and former executive director of the [[Alaska Permanent Fund]] [[Byron Mallott]], whose running mate was State Senator [[Hollis French]]. Also running as an independent was former Republican mayor of [[Valdez, Alaska|Valdez]] [[Bill Walker (American politician)|Bill Walker]], whose running mate was Craig Fleener, the former deputy commissioner of the [[Alaska Department of Fish and Game]]. On September 2, 2014, Walker and Mallott merged their campaigns to appear on the November ballot as a single independent ticket, which the Alaska Democratic Party endorsed. On this ticket, Walker ran for governor with Mallott as his running mate. Both candidates' former running mates withdrew.{{cite news|url=http://www.adn.com/article/20140901/walker-mallott-join-forces-governors-race|title=Walker, Mallott to join forces in governor's race|date=September 1, 2014|access-date=September 2, 2014|publisher=Alaska Dispatch News|archive-date=May 6, 2016|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160506203920/http://www.adn.com/article/20140901/walker-mallott-join-forces-governors-race|url-status=live}} Parnell was considered vulnerable, as reflected in his low approval ratings. The consensus among ''[[The Cook Political Report]]'', ''[[Governing (magazine)|Governing]]'', ''[[Stuart Rothenberg|The Rothenberg Political Report]]'', ''[[Sabato's Crystal Ball]]'', ''Daily Kos Elections'', and others was that the contest was a tossup. Former Republican governor [[Sarah Palin]], who had praised Parnell as her successor when she resigned in 2009, endorsed Walker and Mallott, taking issue with Parnell's tax cuts for the oil and gas industry. On November 7, Walker and Mallott held a 3,165-vote lead,{{cite news|url=http://www.adn.com/article/20141106/governors-race-walker-has-edge-or-maybe-not|title=In governor's race, Walker has edge -- or July 23, 2014. Retrieved October 3, 2014. In October 2014, former Alaska Governor [[Sarah Palin]] endorsed Walker and Mallott. The endorsement was prompted by Parnell's oil and gas industry tax cuts, which dismantled her administration's "Alaska's Clear and Equitable Share" (ACES) plan. She had previously supported a referendum to repeal the tax cuts, which was narrowly defeated{{Cite web|url=https://ballotpedia.org/Alaska_Oil_Tax_Cuts_Veto_Referendum,_Ballot_Measure_1_(August_2014)|title=Alaska Oil Tax Cuts Veto Referendum, Ballot Measure 1 (August 2014)|website=Ballotpedia|access-date=February 16, 2026|archive-date=August 20, 2025|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20250820075438/https://ballotpedia.org/Alaska_Oil_Tax_Cuts_Veto_Referendum,_Ballot_Measure_1_(August_2014)|url-status=live}} in August 2014. Bentley]] | after_party = Republican Party (United States) }} {{Elections in Alabama sidebar}} The '''2014 Alabama gubernatorial election''' took place on November 4, 2014, to elect the [[governor of Alabama]]. Incumbent Governor [[Robert J. Bentley]] won a second term over [[Democratic Party (United States)|Democrat]] [[Parker Griffith]]. This was the first Alabama gubernatorial race where either [[Choctaw County, Alabama|Choctaw]] and/or [[Conecuh County, Alabama|Conecuh]] counties voted Republican. As of 2026, this is the last time [[Jefferson County, Alabama|Jefferson County]] voted Republican in any statewide election contested by a Democrat. Bentley did not complete this term; he resigned in April 2017 due to a scandal and was succeeded by fellow Republican [[Kay Ivey]]. ==Republican primary== ===Candidates=== ====Declared==== * [[Robert J. '''Ross:''' {{legend0|#a5b0ff|40–50%}} {{legend0|#7996e2|50–60%}} {{legend0|#6674de|60–70%}} | title = [[Governor of Arkansas|Governor]] | before_election = [[Mike Beebe]] | before_party = Democratic Party (United States) | after_election = [[Asa Hutchinson]] | after_party = Republican Party (United States) }} {{ElectionsAR}} The '''2014 Arkansas gubernatorial election''' was held on November 4, 2014, to elect the [[governor of Arkansas]], concurrently with the [[2014 United States Senate election in Arkansas|election]] to Arkansas's [[Classes of United States senators|Class II U.S. Senate seat]], as well as other elections to the [[2014 United States Senate elections|United States Senate]] in other states and elections to the [[2014 United States House of Representatives elections|United States House of Representatives]] and various state and local elections. This was the last time the Arkansas governor changed partisan control. Incumbent Governor [[Mike Beebe]] was ineligible to run for re-election due to [[Term limits in the United States|term limits]] established by the [[Constitution of Arkansas|Arkansas Constitution]]. [[Arkansas]] is one of nine states that limit governors to two terms for life.{{cite web|url=http://realclearpolitics.com/news/ap/politics/2011/Dec/05/coleman_mulling_2014_bid_for_ark__governor.html |title=Coleman mulling 2014 bid for Ark. governor |date=December 5, 2011 |work=[[RealClearPolitics]] |first=Andrew |last=Demillo |access-date=December 6, 2011 |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120108145503/http://www.realclearpolitics.com/news/ap/politics/2011/Dec/05/coleman_mulling_2014_bid_for_ark__governor.html |archive-date=January 8, 2012 }} Democrats nominated former U.S. Representative [[Mike Ross (politician)|Mike Ross]] and Republicans nominated former [[Drug Enforcement Administration|DEA]] Administrator, former U.S. Representative and [[2006 Arkansas gubernatorial election|2006]] Arkansas gubernatorial nominee [[Asa Hutchinson]]. This was the only Democratic-held governorship up for election in a state that [[Mitt Romney]] won in the [[2012 United States presidential election in Arkansas|2012 presidential election]]. Hutchinson won the general election by the largest margin recorded for a Republican in an open-seat gubernatorial race since Reconstruction, a record held until 2022. The race was called for Hutchinson roughly half an hour after the polls closed; his victory gave Republicans complete control of state government for the first time since 1874. As of the [[2026 Arkansas gubernatorial election|2026 gubernatorial election]], this is the last time where the following counties voted Democratic: [[Ashley County, Arkansas|Ashley]], [[Bradley {{legend0|#808080|No data}} | title = [[Governor of Arizona|Governor]] | before_election = [[Jan Brewer]] | before_party = Republican Party (United States) | after_election = [[Doug Ducey]] | after_party = Republican Party (United States) | turnout = 47.52% {{decrease}}8.13pp {{Cite web|url=https://azsos.gov/elections/results-data/voter-registration-statistics|title=Voter Registration Statistics | Arizona Secretary of State|accessdate=7 May 2023}} }} {{ElectionsAZ}} The '''2014 Arizona gubernatorial election''' was held on November 4, 2014, to elect the [[governor of Arizona]], concurrently with [[2014 United States Senate elections|elections]] to the [[United States Senate]] in other states and [[2014 United States House of Representatives elections|elections]] to the [[United States House of Representatives]] and various [[2014 United States elections#State elections|state]] and [[2014 United States elections#Local elections|local elections]]. Incumbent [[Republican Party (United States)|Republican]] Governor [[Jan Brewer]] was term-limited and could not run for a second consecutive full term in office. After a competitive six-candidate primary, Republicans nominated [[State Treasurer of Arizona|Arizona State Treasurer]] [[Doug Ducey]]. [[Democratic Party (United States)|Democrat]] [[Fred DuVal]], the former chair of the [[Arizona Board of Regents]], won his party's nomination unopposed. Ducey won the election with 53% of the vote. ==Background== [[File:Arizona 2014 gubernatorial candidates by Gage Skidmore.jpg|right|thumb|250px|Candidates for governor speaking at a forum hosted by the [[Arizona Chamber of Commerce and Industry]]. From left to right: Al Melvin, Scott Smith, Christine Jones, Fred DuVal, Frank Riggs, Doug Ducey and Ken Bennett.]] [[Democratic Party (United States)|Democratic]] governor [[Janet Napolitano]] resigned on January 21, 2009, to be sworn in as [[United States Secretary of Homeland Security|Secretary]] of the [[United States Department of Homeland Security|Department of Homeland Security]]. Since Arizona did not have a [[Lieutenant governor (United States)|lieutenant governor]] at the time, [[Secretary of State of Arizona|Secretary of State]] [[Jan Brewer]] was first in the state's gubernatorial line of succession and was sworn in as governor on the same day. She was elected to a full term [[2010 Arizona gubernatorial election|in 2010]], defeating Democrat [[Terry Goddard]], the [[Arizona Attorney General]], by 54% to 42%. Brewer was term-limited in 2014, despite only serving one full term. This is because Arizona state law limits office holders to two consecutive terms regardless of whether they serve full or partial terms. In November 2012, Brewer declared she was looking into what she called "ambiguity" in Arizona's term-limit law to seek a third term.{{cite news |url=https://www.politico.com/story/2012/11/report-brewer-may-seek-3rd-term-083720 |title= Report: Jan Brewer may seek 3rd term as Arizona governor |work=[[Politico]] |date=November 12, 2012 |access-date=November 13, 2012}} In February 2014, Brewer reiterated that she was considering running for re-election,{{cite news |url=http://www.azcentral.com/news/politics/articles/20140224brewer-hard-let-go-governing-decides-whether-seek-re-election.html |title= Brewer says it's hard to let go of governing as she decides whether to seek re-election |work=AZ Central |date=February 24, 2014 |access-date=March 3, 2014}} but on March 12, 2014, she announced that she would not attempt to seek another term in office, which would have required what ''[[The Arizona Republic]]'' called a "long-shot court challenge".{{cite news |url=http://www.azcentral.com/news/politics/articles/20140312arizona-governor-jan-brewer-not-running-again.html |title= Arizona Gov. 2014 California gubernatorial election.text:
{{Short description|none}} {{see also|2014 United States gubernatorial elections}} {{Use American English|date=January 2025}} {{Use mdy dates|date=September 2013}} {{Infobox election | election_name = 2014 California gubernatorial election | country = California | type = presidential | ongoing = no | previous_election = 2010 California gubernatorial election | previous_year = 2010 | next_election = 2018 California gubernatorial election | next_year = 2018 | election_date = November 4, 2014 | turnout = 30.94% ({{decrease}}28.65 [[Percentage point|pp]]) | image_size = 150x150px | image1 = Governor Jerry Brown 2015.jpg | candidate1 = '''[[Jerry Brown]]''' | party1 = California Democratic Party | popular_vote1 = '''4,388,368''' | percentage1 = '''59.97%''' | image2 = File:Neel-kashkari (3x4a).jpg | candidate2 = [[Neel Kashkari]] | party2 = California Republican Party | popular_vote2 = 2,929,213 | percentage2 = 40.03% | map_image = {{switcher |[[File:2014 California gubernatorial election results map by county.svg|300px]] | County results |[[File:2014 California gubernatorial election results map by Congressional District.svg|300px]] | Congressional district results}} | map_caption = '''Brown:''' {{legend0|#7996e2|50–60%}} {{legend0|#6674de|60–70%}} {{legend0|#584cde|70–80%}} {{legend0|#3933e5|80–90%}} {{legend0|#0D0596|>90%}}
'''Kashkari:''' {{legend0|#e27f7f|50–60%}} {{legend0|#d75d5d|60–70%}} {{legend0|#d72f30|70–80%}} | title = [[Governor of California|Governor]] | before_election = [[Jerry Brown]] | before_party = Democratic Party (United States) | after_election = [[Jerry Brown]] | after_party = Democratic Party (United States) | map_size = 302px }} {{ElectionsCA}} The '''2014 California gubernatorial election''' was held on November 4, 2014, to elect the [[governor of California]], concurrently with [[2014 California elections|elections]] for the rest of [[California executive branch|California's executive branch]], as well as elections to the [[2014 United States Senate elections|United States Senate]] in other states and elections to the [[2014 United States House of Representatives elections|United States House of Representatives]] and various state and local elections. Incumbent [[California Democratic Party|Democratic]] Governor [[Jerry Brown]] ran for election to a second consecutive and fourth overall term in office. Although governors are limited to lifetime service of two terms in office, Brown previously served as governor from 1975 to 1983, and the law only affects terms served after November 6, 1990.{{cite web|title=Summary of Qualifications and Requirements for the Offices of Governor and Lieutenant Governor |publisher=California Secretary of State Department |url=http://www.sos.ca.gov/elections/statewide-elections/2014-primary/governor-lieutenant-governor-2014.htm |access-date=May 24, 2014 |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140706120012/http://www.sos.ca.gov/elections/statewide-elections/2014-primary/governor-lieutenant-governor-2014.htm |archive-date=July 6, 2014 |df=mdy }}{{cite web|title=Campaign Finance: Brown For Governor 2014|url=http://cal-access.sos.ca.gov/Campaign/Committees/Detail.aspx?id=1333789&session=2013|work=California Secretary of State|access-date=August 6, 2013}}{{cite web|title=Brown Shows Early Lead for 2014 California Gubernatorial Race|url=http://ivn.us/california/2013/08/05/brown-shows-early-lead-for-2014-california-gubernatorial-race/|work=IVN|access-date=August 6, 2013|archive-date=August 8, 2013|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20130808051414/http://ivn.us/california/2013/08/05/brown-shows-early-lead-for-2014-california-gubernatorial-race/|url-status=dead}} A primary election was held on June 3, 2014. Under California's [[nonpartisan blanket primary]] law, all candidates appear on the same ballot, regardless of party. In the primary, voters may vote for any candidate, regardless of their party affiliation. The top two finishers — regardless of party — advance to the general election in November, even if a candidate manages to receive a majority of the votes cast in the primary election. [[Washington (state)|Washington]] is the only other state with this system, a top two primary ([[Louisiana]] has a similar primary). Brown and Republican [[Neel Kashkari]] finished first and second, respectively,{{cite web|title=Governor: Tim Donnelly congratulates Neel Kashkari|url=http://www.sacbee.com/2014/06/03/6455696/governor-neel-kashkari-leads-tim.html|work=IVN|access-date=June 4, 2014|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140604225558/http://www.sacbee.com/2014/06/03/6455696/governor-neel-kashkari-leads-tim.html|archive-date=June 4, 2014|url-status=dead}} which Brown won. He won the largest gubernatorial victory since [[1986 California gubernatorial election|1986]], "despite running a virtually nonexistent campaign."{{cite web|title=Jerry Brown Coasts To Re-Election With Nonexistent Campaign| date=November 5, 2014 |publisher=Huffington Post|url=https://www.huffingtonpost.com/2014/11/04/california-governor-election-results_n_5819772.html|access-date=November 30, 2014}} This was the first time since [[1978 California gubernatorial election|1978]] that a Democrat carried Nevada County. ==Primary election== [[File:Neel Kashkari marching in the 2014 San Diego LGBT Pride Parade (1).jpg|thumb|right|Republican candidate Kashkari campaigns at the San Diego LGBT Pride Parade.]] A certified list of candidates was released by the secretary of state on March 27, 2014. '''Beauprez:''' {{legend0|#ffb2b2|40–50%}} {{legend0|#e27f7f|50–60%}} {{legend0|#d75d5d|60–70%}} {{legend0|#d72f30|70–80%}} {{legend0|#c21b18|80–90%}} | title = [[Governor of Colorado|Governor]] | before_election = [[John Hickenlooper]] | before_party = Democratic Party (United States) | after_election = [[John Hickenlooper]] | after_party = Democratic Party (United States) }} {{ElectionsCO}} The '''2014 Colorado gubernatorial election''' was held on November 4, 2014, to elect the [[Governor of Colorado|governor]] and [[Lieutenant Governor of Colorado|lieutenant governor of Colorado]], concurrently with the [[United States Senate election in Colorado, 2014|election]] to Colorado's [[Classes of United States senators|Class II U.S. Senate seat]], as well as other elections to the [[2014 United States Senate elections|United States Senate]] in other states and elections to the [[2014 United States House of Representatives elections|United States House of Representatives]] and various state and local elections. Incumbent [[Democratic Party (United States)|Democratic]] Governor [[John Hickenlooper]] and Lieutenant Governor [[Joseph Garcia (American politician)|Joseph Garcia]] were elected to a second term in office, narrowly defeating [[Republican Party (United States)|Republican]] former U.S. representative [[Bob Beauprez]] and his running mate, [[Douglas County, Colorado|Douglas County]] [[County commission|Commissioner]] Jill Repella, by 68,000 votes. ==Democratic primary== John Hickenlooper was the only Democrat to file to run, and thus at the Democratic state assembly on April 12, 2014, he was renominated unopposed. ===Candidates=== ====Nominee==== * [[John Hickenlooper]], incumbent governor{{cite web|url=http://www.denverpost.com/news/ci_25554780/flood-recovery-rallies-democrats-they-renominate-hick-udall|title=Flood recovery rallies Democrats as they renominate Hick, Udall|date=April 12, 2014|access-date=April 13, 2014|work=[[The Denver Post]]|first=Alison|last=Noon}}{{cite web|url=http://gazette.com/sunrise-hickenlooper-in-rural-colorado-as-2014-race-begins/article/1504824|title=SUNRISE: Hickenlooper in rural Colorado as 2014 race begins|date=August 15, 2013|access-date=August 15, 2013|work=The Gazette}} ===Results=== {{Election box begin no change | title = Democratic primary results{{cite web|url=http://results.enr.clarityelections.com/CO/51557/135090/en/summary.html#|title=CO – Election Results|access-date=November 24, 2014}} }} {{Election box winning candidate with party link no change | candidate = John Hickenlooper (incumbent) | party = Democratic Party (United States) | votes = 214,403 | percentage = 100.00 }} {{Election box total no change | votes = 214,403 | percentage= 100.00 }} {{Election box end}} ==Republican primary== At the Republican state assembly on April 12, 2014, [[Mike Kopp]] and [[Scott Gessler]] received 34% and 33% of the votes of over 3,900 delegates, respectively, thus winning a place on the ballot. [[Greg Brophy]], Steve House and Roni Bell Sylvester received 19%, 13% and 2%, respectively, falling short of the 30% needed to qualify for the ballot. [[Bob Beauprez]] and [[Tom Tancredo]] did not contest the assembly vote, instead petitioning their way onto the ballot.{{cite web|url=http://www.denverpost.com/news/ci_25553402/u-s-rep-cory-gardner-clear-favorite-become|title=Rep. Foley]] | running_mate2 = [[Heather Somers]] | party2 = Republican Party (United States) | alliance2 = [[Independent Party of Connecticut|Independent]] | popular_vote2 = 526,295 | percentage2 = 48.16% }} {{ElectionsCT}} The '''2014 Connecticut gubernatorial election''' took place on November 4, 2014, to elect the [[List of governors of Connecticut|governor]] and [[Lieutenant Governor of Connecticut|lieutenant governor of Connecticut]], concurrently with [[2014 United States Senate elections|elections]] to the [[United States Senate]] in other states and [[2014 United States House of Representatives elections|elections]] to the [[United States House of Representatives]] and various [[2014 United States elections#State elections|state]] and [[2014 United States elections#Local elections|local elections]]. Incumbent Democratic Governor [[Dannel Malloy]] won re-election to a second term in office. Connecticut, unlike most states, holds separate primary elections for governor and lieutenant governor, with the winners then running together on the same ticket. Malloy and incumbent Lieutenant Governor [[Nancy Wyman]] were renominated unopposed. The Republicans nominated former [[United States Ambassador to Ireland|U.S. Ambassador to Ireland]] and nominee for governor [[2010 Connecticut gubernatorial election|in 2010]] [[Thomas C. Foley]] and [[Groton, Connecticut|Groton]] Town Councilor [[Heather Somers]], making the contest a rematch of the 2010 election. [[Independent politician|Independent]] candidate Joe Visconti, a former [[West Hartford, Connecticut|West Hartford]] Town Councilor and the Republican nominee for [[Connecticut's 1st congressional district]] in [[United States House of Representatives elections in Connecticut, 2008#District 1|2008]] was running with Chester Harris, a former Republican [[Haddam, Connecticut|Haddam]] School Board Member. Visconti suspended his campaign on November 2 and endorsed Foley. However, due to the suspension coming only two days before the election, Visconti's name remained on the ballot. Former State Representative Jonathan Pelto (D-Mansfield){{Cite web|url=http://patch.com/connecticut/mansfield/jonathan-pelto-announces-candidacy-for-governor|title = Jonathan Pelto Announces Candidacy for Governor|date = 12 June 2014}} explored a third-party candidacy through a petition drive but was disqualified due to an inadequate number of signatures.{{Cite web|url=http://ctmirror.org/2014/08/29/pelto-falls-3200-signatures-short-of-spot-on-ct-gubernatorial-ballot/|title = Pelto falls 3,200 signatures short of spot on CT gubernatorial ballot|date = 29 August 2014}} ==Democratic primary== ===Governor=== ====Candidates==== =====Declared===== * [[Dannel Malloy]], incumbent Governor{{cite web|title=Yes, Dan Malloy is running in 2014|url=http://ctmirror.org/yes-malloy-is-running/|access-date=30 March 2014|date=28 March 2014|publisher=Ctmirror.org}} ====Withdrew==== * Lee Whitnum, writer, candidate for [[Connecticut's 4th congressional district]] in [[United States House of Representatives elections in Connecticut, 2008#District 4|2008]] and candidate for the U.S. Senate in [[United States Senate election in Connecticut, 2010|2010]] and [[United States Senate election in Connecticut, 2012|2012]]{{cite web|url=http://www.greenwichtime.com/local/article/Whitnum-says-she-s-running-for-governor-5326104.php|title=Whitnum says she's running for governor|date=March 17, 2014|access-date=March 19, 2014|work=[[Greenwich Time (newspaper)|Greenwich Time]]|first=Neil|last=Vigdor}} ===Lieutenant governor=== ====Candidates==== =====Declared===== * [[Nancy Wyman]], incumbent Lieutenant Governor ===Results=== Malloy and Wyman ran unopposed for the Democratic nomination, so no primaries were held. ==Republican primary== ===Governor=== 2010 nominee Thomas C. Foley won the endorsement of the state party at the Republican State Convention on May 17, winning 57.1% of the vote.{{cite web|url=http://www.ctpost.com/local/article/Foley-gets-GOP-nod-but-Boughton-and-McKinney-to-5486239.php|title=Foley gets GOP nod, but Boughton and McKinney to primary|date=May 18, 2014|access-date=May 19, 2014|work=[[Connecticut Post]]|first=Neil|last=Vigdor}} Danbury Mayor Mark Boughton and State Senate Minority Leader John McKinney took 22.3% and 17.72%, respectively, meeting the 15% vote threshold and thus also qualified for the primary ballot.{{cite web|url=https://www.courant.com/2014/05/17/gop-nominates-foley-for-governor-boughton-mckinney-qualify-for-primary/|title=GOP Nominates Foley For Governor; Boughton, McKinney Qualify For Primary|date=May 17, 2014|access-date=May 20, 2014|work=The Courant}} Shelton Mayor Mark Lauretti and former [[West Hartford, Connecticut|West Hartford]] Town Councilor Joe Visconti failed to get 15% of the vote at the convention, so neither automatically qualified for the ballot. Visconti began collecting signatures to petition his way onto the ballot. He needed the signatures of 8,190 registered Republican voters by June 10 in order to qualify and he started collecting signatures when primary petitions became available at the end of April.{{cite news|last=Stuart|first=Christine|title=Visconti To Petition His Way Onto Primary Ballot|url=http://www.ctnewsjunkie.com/archives/entry/visconti_to_petition_his_way_onto_primary_ballot/|access-date=May 25, 2014|newspaper=CT News Junkie|date=April 24, 2014}} Lauretti began to collect signatures a few days after the convention, but withdrew those petitions on May 22 to instead try to petition onto the ballot for lieutenant governor.{{cite news|title=Lauretti Drops Down To Lieutenant Governor Race|url=http://www.ctnewsjunkie.com/archives/entry/lauretti_drops_down_to_lieutenant_governor_race/|access-date=May 25, 2014|newspaper=CT News Junkie|date=May 22, 2014|author=Staff Report}} On June 6, Visconti announced that he was short of the required number of signatures, and with the filing deadline only 4 days away, was withdrawing from the race to run as an independent instead.{{cite web|url=http://ctmirror.org/visconti-ends-gop-campaign-to-run-as-unaffiliated/|title=Visconti ends GOP campaign to run as independent|date=June 6, 2014|access-date=June 19, 2014|work=[[The Connecticut Mirror]]|last=Pazniokas|first=Mark}} Boughton suspended his campaign on June 18, primarily because he did not think Lauretti, his unofficial running mate, would qualify for the ballot, which would have meant Boughton failing to qualify for public financing.{{cite news|title=Lauretti fails to qualify for lieutenant governor primary|url=http://www.thewestonforum.com/19386/lauretti-fails-to-qualify-for-lieutenant-governor-primary/|access-date=August 28, 2014|publisher=The Weston Forum|date=June 26, 2014|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140903081117/http://www.thewestonforum.com/19386/lauretti-fails-to-qualify-for-lieutenant-governor-primary/|archive-date=September 3, 2014|url-status=dead}} He called for "party unity behind the endorsed Republican candidate, Tom Foley."{{cite news|title=Mark Boughton Calls Off Campaign for Governor|url=http://www.nbcconnecticut.com/news/local/Mark-Boughton-Suspends-Campaign-for-Governor-263688601.html|access-date=July 1, 2014|newspaper=NBC Connecticut|date=June 18, 2014}} Heather Bond Somers had originally been running on such a "ticket" with Mark Boughton,{{cite web|url=http://www.connecticutmag.com/Mark-Boughton-Taps-Groton-Mayor-Heather-Bond-Somers-as-Running-Mate/|title=Mark Boughton Taps Heather Bond Somers as Running Mate|date=28 January 2014|access-date=27 May 2014|work=Connecticut Mag|author=Jennifer Swift}} but she withdrew from the arrangement.{{cite web|url=http://www.nhregister.com/government-and-politics/20140522/somers-dumps-boughton-as-running-mate-in-republican-race|title=Somers dumps Boughton as running mate in Republican race|date=22 May 2014|access-date=27 May 2014|work=New Haven Register|author=Mary E. David M. Walker teamed up with John P. McKinney.{{cite web|url=http://ctmirror.org/mckinney-walker-ticket-promises-positive-gop-primary/|title=McKinney, Walker form ticket, then each finishes third|date=17 May 2014|access-date=27 May 2014|work=CT Mirror|author=Mark Pazniokas}} Bacchiochi did not join any "ticket".{{cite web|url=http://www.ctnewsjunkie.com/archives/entry/bacchiochi_wins_nomination/|title=Bacchiochi Wins GOP Lt. Gov. Nomination|date=17 May 2014|access-date=27 May 2014|work=CT News Junkie}} Bacchiochi won the endorsement of the state party at the Republican State Convention on May 17, winning 50.9% of the vote. Somers took 31.5% and Walker got 17.4%, meaning they both also qualified for the primary ballot. '''Crist:''' {{legend0|#a5b0ff|40–50%}} {{legend0|#7996e2|50–60%}} {{legend0|#6674de|60–70%}} {{legend0|#584cde|70–80%}} {{legend0|#3933E5|80–90%}} | title = [[List of Governors of Florida|Governor]] | before_election = [[Rick Scott]] | before_party = Republican Party (United States) | after_election = [[Rick Scott]] | after_party = Republican Party (United States) | turnout = 50.5%{{increase}}1.8{{cite web|url=https://results.elections.myflorida.com/Index.asp?ElectionDate=11/4/2014&DATAMODE=|title=November 4, 2014 General Election|website=Florida Department of State|access-date=2022-05-15|archive-date=December 14, 2018|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20181214164429/https://results.elections.myflorida.com/Index.asp?ElectionDate=11/4/2014&DATAMODE=|url-status=dead}} }} {{ElectionsFL}}{{Rick Scott series}}The '''2014 Florida gubernatorial election''' took place on November 4, 2014, to elect the [[List of Governors of Florida|Governor]] and [[Lieutenant Governor of Florida]]. The incumbent [[Republican Party of Florida|Republican]],{{cite web |url=http://www.ocala.com/article/20111004/WIRE/111009899 |title=Gov. Scott: I'll run again in 2014 |publisher=Ocala.com |access-date=March 7, 2013 |archive-date=September 24, 2015 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150924122355/http://www.ocala.com/article/20111004/WIRE/111009899 |url-status=dead }} [[Rick Scott]], ran for reelection. The [[Florida Democratic Party|Democratic]] nominee was former Governor [[Charlie Crist]], who was Scott's direct predecessor. Crist was elected governor as a Republican in [[2006 Florida gubernatorial election|2006]] but did not run for re-election in 2010, instead opting to [[2010 United States Senate election in Florida|run for Senate]] as an [[Independent politician|independent]]. [[Libertarian Party of Florida|Libertarian]] nominee [[Adrian Wyllie]] and several candidates with no party affiliation also ran. Political pundits considered the race a toss-up. This was one of nine Republican-held governorships up for election in a state that [[Barack Obama]] won in the [[2012 United States presidential election|2012 presidential election]]. likely Democratic nominee. Although the ads resulted in a tightening of the race, this came about by decreasing Crist's favorability ratings. By contrast, Scott's favorability ratings did not increase.{{cite web|url=https://www.orlandosentinel.com/2014/06/08/gov-scotts-ad-blitz-aims-to-hit-crist-early/ |title=Gov. Scott's ad blitz aims to hit Crist early |publisher=Orlando Sentinel |date=June 8, 2014 |access-date=July 18, 2014 |author=Aaron Deslatte}} By late September, Scott's television ad spending had exceeded $35 million,{{cite web |url=http://www.therepublic.com/view/story/dc58e5b58f32444e82eb6a2238814122/FL--Governors-Race-Campaign |title=Florida Gov. Rick Scott and ex-Gov. Charlie Crist bash each other as campaigns kick into gear |work=The Republic |date=September 1, 2014 |access-date=September 20, 2014 |author=Gary Fineout |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140914004332/http://www.therepublic.com/view/story/dc58e5b58f32444e82eb6a2238814122/FL--Governors-Race-Campaign |archive-date=September 14, 2014 |url-status=dead |df=mdy-all }}{{cite web|url=http://www.miamiherald.com/news/local/news-columns-blogs/marc-caputo/article2194752.html |title=Marc Caputo: With $50 million in TV ad spending, Rick Scott-Charlie Crist race is one big marketing campaign |work=Miami Herald |date=September 21, 2014 |access-date=September 23, 2014 |author=Marc Caputo}} and in mid-October it reached $56.5 million, compared to $26.5 million by Crist. On October 22 it was reported that Scott's total spending had exceeded $83 million and he announced that, having previously said he would not do so, he would be investing his own money into the campaign, speculated to be as much as $22 million.{{cite web|url=http://miamiherald.typepad.com/nakedpolitics/2014/10/scott-says-he-will-write-his-campaign-a-personal-check-after-all-.html |title=Scott says he will write his campaign a personal check, after all, but won't say how much |publisher=Miami Herald |date=October 22, 2014 |access-date=October 23, 2014 |author=Marc Caputo}} Crist hoped to draw strong support from Florida's more than 1.6 million registered black voters, an effort that was challenging with regards to his previous political career as a Republican. A poll conducted in September 2014 by Quinnipiac University revealed his support among black voters was at 72 percent against Scott, which was below the 90 percent analysts believed he needed to win.{{cite news|last1=Stein|first1=Letitia|title=In Florida governor's race, Democrat woos crucial black vote|url=https://www.reuters.com/article/us-usa-florida-election-idUSKBN0FZ17J20140730|access-date=September 15, 2014|work=Reuters|date=July 30, 2014}} Scott and Crist met in a debate on October 15, held by the Florida Press Association at [[Broward College]].{{cite web| url=http://beforeyouvote.org/| title=The race for the governor of florida| website=Before You Vote| access-date=October 5, 2014}} The debate required candidates to receive at least 15% support in major polls to be included. This was allegedly increased from 10% after Wyllie met the initial criteria,{{cite web| url=http://www.uncoveredpolitics.com/2014/09/18/despite-strong-polling-libertarian-barred-from-florida-gubernatorial-debate/| title=Despite Strong Polling, Libertarian Barred from Florida Gubernatorial Debate | date=September 18, 2014| website =Uncovered Politics| access-date =October 5, 2014}} but the ''Miami Herald'' reported that the threshold had been 15% since 2013.{{cite news | url=http://miamiherald.typepad.com/nakedpolitics/2014/10/libertarian-adrian-wyllie-sues-to-get-into-florida-press-association-debate.html | title=Libertarian Adrian Wyllie sues to get into Florida Press Association debate | work=Miami Herald | date=October 9, 2014 | author=Caputo. '''Tie:''' {{legend0|#d2b1d9|40–50%}} {{legend0|#ae8bb1|50%}} {{legend0|#808080|No data}} | title = [[Governor of Georgia|Governor]] | before_election = [[Nathan Deal]] | before_party = Republican Party (United States) | after_election = [[Nathan Deal]] | after_party = Republican Party (United States) }} {{ElectionsGA}} The '''2014 Georgia gubernatorial election''' took place on November 4, 2014, to elect the [[governor of Georgia]], concurrently with the [[United States Senate election in Georgia, 2014|election]] to Georgia's [[Classes of United States senators|Class II U.S. Senate seat]], [[2014 United States Senate elections|elections]] to the United States Senate in other states, [[2014 United States House of Representatives elections|elections]] to the [[United States House of Representatives]], and various [[2014 United States elections#State elections|state]] and [[2014 United States elections#Local elections|local elections]]. Incumbent [[Republican Party (United States)|Republican]] Governor [[Nathan Deal]] was elected to a second term in office by a margin of 7.8%. He defeated two primary challengers, and in the general election defeated [[Democratic Party (United States)|Democratic]] state Senator [[Jason Carter (politician)|Jason Carter]] and [[Libertarian Party (United States)|Libertarian]] nominee businessman and engineer Andrew Hunt, who were unopposed in their respective primaries. Despite Carter's loss, he flipped [[Douglas County, Georgia|Douglas County]], [[Henry County, Georgia|Henry County]], and [[Newton County, Georgia|Newton County]]. As of 2022, this is the last time that [[Cobb County, Georgia|Cobb]] and [[Gwinnett County, Georgia|Gwinnett]] counties voted for the Republican candidate for governor, and the last time that [[Chattahoochee County, Georgia|Chattahoochee]], [[Dooly County, Georgia|Dooly]], [[Quitman County, Georgia|Quitman]], [[Twiggs County, Georgia|Twiggs]], and [[Wilkinson County, Georgia|Wilkinson]] counties voted for the Democratic candidate. {{legend0|#808080|No votes}} | title = [[Governor of Hawaii|Governor]] | before_election = [[Neil Abercrombie]] | before_party = Democratic Party (United States) | after_election = [[David Ige]] | after_party = Democratic Party (United States) }} {{ElectionsHI}} The '''2014 Hawaii gubernatorial election''' took place on November 4, 2014, to elect the [[Governor of Hawaii]], concurrently with a [[United States Senate election in Hawaii, 2014|special election]] to Hawaii's [[Classes of United States senators|Class III]] [[United States Senate|Senate Seat]], as well as other elections to the [[2014 United States Senate elections|United States Senate]] in other states and elections to the [[2014 United States House of Representatives elections|United States House of Representatives]] and various state and local elections. Primary elections were held on August 9, 2014. In Hawaii, candidates for governor and lieutenant governor run in separate primaries and are then elected on the same ticket. Incumbent Democratic governor [[Neil Abercrombie]] ran for re-election to a second term in office, but was defeated by [[Hawaii Senate|State Senator]] [[David Ige]] in the Democratic primary, making Abercrombie the first incumbent governor to lose renomination in Hawaii history. Incumbent Democratic [[Lieutenant Governor of Hawaii|lieutenant governor]] [[Shan Tsutsui]] was renominated. The Republicans nominated former [[Lieutenant Governor of Hawaii|lieutenant governor]] [[Duke Aiona]] and pastor and former circuit court judge Elwin Ahu. Also running as an independent was former [[mayor of Honolulu]] [[Mufi Hannemann]] and former Honolulu parks and recreation director Les Chang. Ige and Tsutsui won the election. This would be the last election until [[2026 Rhode Island gubernatorial election|2026]] in which an elected incumbent state governor lost renomination.{{efn|Governor [[Jeff Colyer]] of Kansas, who had taken office after the resignation of [[Sam Brownback]], was defeated by [[Kris Kobach]] in the [[2018 Kansas gubernatorial election|2018]] Republican primary election.}} ==Democratic primary== ===Governor=== ====Candidates==== '''Declared''' * [[Neil Abercrombie]], incumbent governor{{cite news |url=http://www.bizjournals.com/pacific/news/2013/04/29/hawaii-gov-neil-abercrombie-says-he.html |title=Hawaii Gov. Republican incumbent [[Terry Branstad]] ran for reelection to a sixth overall and second consecutive four-year term.{{cite web|title=Governor Terry Branstad announces gubernatorial run, tours Iowa|url=http://www.kwwl.com/story/24450784/2014/01/14/governor-terry-branstad-to-tour-iowa-make-special-announcement|work=KWWL|access-date=15 January 2014|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140116135037/http://www.kwwl.com/story/24450784/2014/01/14/governor-terry-branstad-to-tour-iowa-make-special-announcement|archive-date=16 January 2014|url-status=dead}} Branstad went on to win a historic sixth term as governor by defeating Democratic challenger and State Senator [[Jack Hatch]], and on December 14, 2015, he became the longest-serving governor in American history. He won 59.1% of the popular vote to Hatch's 37.3%, and carried every county in the state except [[Johnson County, Iowa|Johnson]], home to [[Iowa City, Iowa|Iowa City]] and the [[University of Iowa]]. '''Tie:''' {{legend0|#DECDE6|40–50%}} {{legend0|#b3b3b3|No votes}} | title = [[Governor of Illinois|Governor]] | before_election = [[Pat Quinn (politician)|Pat Quinn]] | before_party = Democratic Party (United States) | after_election = [[Bruce Rauner]] | after_party = Republican Party (United States) | turnout = 48.48% {{decrease}} 1.21 [[percentage point|pp]] }} {{ElectionsIL}} The '''2014 Illinois gubernatorial election''' was held on November 4, 2014, to elect the [[Governor of Illinois|governor]] and [[Lieutenant Governor of Illinois|lieutenant governor of Illinois]], concurrently with the [[2014 United States Senate election in Illinois|election]] to Illinois's [[Classes of United States senators|Class II U.S. Senate seat]], as well as other elections to the [[2014 United States Senate elections|United States Senate]] in other states and elections to the [[2014 United States House of Representatives elections|United States House of Representatives]] and various state and local elections. Before this cycle, candidates for governor and lieutenant governor were nominated separately, and the primary winners ran on the same ticket in the general election. In 2011, the law was changed to allow candidates for governor to pick their own running mates. Incumbent Democratic Lieutenant Governor [[Sheila Simon]] did not run for reelection, instead running unsuccessfully [[2014 Illinois elections#Comptroller|for comptroller]]. She was replaced as Quinn's running mate by [[Paul Vallas]], a former [[Chief Executive Officer of Chicago Public Schools|CEO]] of [[Chicago Public Schools]]. Rauner chose [[Wheaton, Illinois|Wheaton]] City councilwoman [[Evelyn Sanguinetti]] as his running mate and Grimm chose Alex Cummings. Incumbent [[Democratic Party (United States)|Democratic]] governor [[Pat Quinn (politician)|Pat Quinn]] ran for re-election to a second full term in office. Quinn, then the lieutenant governor, assumed the office of governor on January 29, 2009, upon the [[Impeachment in the United States|impeachment]] and removal of [[Rod Blagojevich]]. He narrowly won a full term in [[2010 Illinois gubernatorial election|2010]]. Primary elections were held on March 18, 2014.{{cite web |url=http://www.elections.illinois.gov/ |title=Illinois State Board of Elections |publisher=Elections.illinois.gov |access-date=2015-01-09 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150331040020/http://www.elections.illinois.gov/ |archive-date=2015-03-31 |url-status=dead }} Quinn won the Democratic primary, while the [[Republican Party (United States)|Republicans]] chose businessman [[Bruce Rauner]] and the [[Libertarian Party (United States)|Libertarians]] nominated political activist Chad Grimm. Rauner defeated Quinn in the general election with 50.3% of the vote to Quinn's 46.4%, winning every county in the state except for [[Cook County]], home to the city of [[Chicago]] and 40% of the state's residents.{{cite web|url= https://www.huffpost.com/entry/pat-quinn-concedes_n_6110092|title=Pat Quinn Concedes Illinois Gubernatorial Race to Bruce Rauner|work=[[Huffington Post]]|date=November 5, 2014|archive-date= November 6, 2014|archive-url= https://web.archive.org/web/20141106202708/https://www.huffingtonpost.com/2014/11/05/pat-quinn-concedes_n_6110092.html|url-status= live|access-date=November 6, 2014}}Newman, James (November 5, 2014) - [http://www.niutoday.info/2014/11/05/think-quinnrauner-was-a-squeaker-and-durbinoberweis-was-a-cakewalk-heres-why-youd-be-wrong/ "Quinn/Rauner a Squeaker? ''Northern Illinois University''. Retrieved December 5, 2014. Quinn was the only incumbent Democratic governor to lose a general election in 2014 and remained the last one to do so until [[Nevada]]'s [[Steve Sisolak]] in [[2022 Nevada gubernatorial election|2022]]. Rauner became the second Republican to be elected governor of Illinois while carrying all but one county, the other being [[Jim Edgar]] in [[1994 Illinois gubernatorial election|1994]]. This was the only time since 1998 that a Republican was elected Governor of Illinois. As of {{CURRENTYEAR}}, this alongside the concurrent comptroller election is the only time since 2010 that Republicans won a statewide election in Illinois. This is also the most recent Illinois gubernatorial election in which the winner won a majority of counties or won by a single-digit margin. Quinn later ran for Illinois Attorney General in [[2018 Illinois Attorney General election|2018]] and lost the Democratic primary. ==Background== The primaries and general elections coincided with those for federal ([[2014 United States House of Representatives elections in Illinois|House]] and [[2014 United States Senate election in Illinois|Senate]]) and those for other state offices. '''Davis:''' {{legend0|#a5b0ff|40–50%}} {{legend0|#7996e2|50–60%}} {{legend0|#6674de|60–70%}} {{legend0|#584cde|70–80%}} | title = [[Governor of Kansas|Governor]] | before_election = [[Sam Brownback]] | before_party = Republican Party (United States) | after_election = [[Sam Brownback]] | after_party = Republican Party (United States) | image2_size = 150x150px }} {{ElectionsKS}} The '''2014 Kansas gubernatorial election''' took place on November 4, 2014, to elect the [[List of governors of Kansas|governor of Kansas]]. It was held concurrently with the [[2014 United States Senate election in Kansas|election]] of Kansas' [[Classes of United States senators|Class II U.S. Senate seat]], elections to the [[2014 United States Senate elections|United States Senate]] in other states, elections to the [[2014 United States House of Representatives elections|United States House of Representatives]], and various state and local elections. Incumbent [[Republican Party (United States)|Republican]] governor [[Sam Brownback]] ran for re-election to a second term. He was opposed in the general election by [[Democratic Party (United States)|Democrat]] [[Paul Davis (Kansas politician)|Paul Davis]], the minority leader of the [[Kansas House of Representatives]], and Libertarian attorney Keen Umbehr. The election was viewed as a referendum on Brownback's [[Kansas experiment|aggressive tax cutting initiatives]] and his conservative values.{{cite web|url=http://kansasfirstnews.com/2014/11/04/brownback-defeats-davis-in-kansas-governors-race|title=Brownback defeats Davis in Kansas Governor's race|access-date=2014-11-14|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20141129151708/http://kansasfirstnews.com/2014/11/04/brownback-defeats-davis-in-kansas-governors-race/|archive-date=2014-11-29|url-status=dead}} The consensus among ''[[The Cook Political Report]]'', ''[[Governing (magazine)|Governing]]'', ''[[Stuart Rothenberg|The Rothenberg Political Report]]'', ''[[Sabato's Crystal Ball]]'', ''Daily Kos Elections'', and others was that the contest was a tossup. Brownback won the election by a margin of 3.69%. Davis carried seven counties, all in eastern Kansas. As of 2026, this is the last time a Republican, and a male was elected Governor of Kansas. ==Republican primary== ===Candidates=== ====Declared==== * [[Sam Brownback]], incumbent [[Governor of Kansas|governor]]{{cite web|url=https://www2.ljworld.com/weblogs/capitol-report/2013/jun/21/brownback-running-for-re-election/|title=Brownback running for re-election|work=[[Lawrence Journal-World]]|date=21 June 2013|access-date=16 August 2013}} :*Running mate: [[Jeff Colyer]], incumbent [[Lieutenant Governor of Kansas|lieutenant governor]] * Jennifer Winn, businesswoman{{cite web|url=http://www.kake.com/news/coveringkakeland/headlines/Wichita-woman-enters-governors-race-239776441.html|title=Wichita woman enters governor's race|work=[[KAKE]]|date=January 12, 2014|access-date=March 31, 2014|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140325001342/http://www.kake.com/news/coveringkakeland/headlines/Wichita-woman-enters-governors-race-239776441.html|archive-date=March 25, 2014|url-status=dead|df=mdy-all}} :*Running mate: Robin Lais, advertising agency owner and natural healing shop owner{{cite web|url=http://www.kansas.com/2014/06/02/3488915/wichita-candidate-for-governor.html|archive-url=https://archive.today/20140626022032/http://www.kansas.com/2014/06/02/3488915/wichita-candidate-for-governor.html|url-status=dead|archive-date=June 26, 2014|title=Wichita candidate for governor announces new running mate|work=[[The Wichita Eagle]]|last=Benchaabane|first=Nassim|date=June 2, 2014|access-date=June 25, 2014}} :*Former running mate: Ethan McCord, Iraq War veteran{{cite web|url=http://pressreleases.kcstar.com/release/messages/59254/|title=Wikileaks Soldier to Run for Ks Lt. '''Tie:''' {{legend0|#d2b1d9|40–50%}} | title = [[Governor of Massachusetts|Governor]] | before_election = [[Deval Patrick]] | before_party = Democratic Party (United States) | after_election = [[Charlie Baker]] | after_party = Republican Party (United States) }} {{ElectionsMA}} The '''2014 Massachusetts gubernatorial election''' took place on November 4, 2014, to elect the [[governor of Massachusetts]], concurrently with [[2014 United States Senate election in Massachusetts|the election]] of Massachusetts's [[Classes of United States senators|Class II U.S. Senate seat]], [[2014 United States Senate elections|other elections]] to the United States Senate in other states, [[2014 United States House of Representatives elections|elections]] to the [[United States House of Representatives]], and various [[2014 United States elections#State elections|state]] and [[2014 United States elections#Local elections|local elections]]. Incumbent [[Democratic Party (United States)|Democratic]] Governor [[Deval Patrick]] was eligible to seek a third term but stated in January 2011 that he would not run for re-election.{{cite news | title=With Charlie Baker on the job hunt, GOP chair hints at 2014 run | url=http://www.masslive.com/news/index.ssf/2010/12/with_charlie_baker_on_the_job.html | work=State House News Service | date=December 20, 2010 | access-date=February 1, 2011 }}{{cite news | first=Noah | last=Bierman | title=Patrick plans to expand travels | url=http://www.boston.com/news/local/massachusetts/articles/2011/01/05/patrick_plans_to_expand_travels_during_second_term | archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20121102225427/http://www.boston.com/news/local/massachusetts/articles/2011/01/05/patrick_plans_to_expand_travels_during_second_term/ | url-status=dead | archive-date=November 2, 2012 | work=Boston Globe | date=January 5, 2011 | access-date=February 1, 2011}} The office of [[Lieutenant Governor of Massachusetts|lieutenant governor]] had been vacant since the resignation of [[Tim Murray]] in June 2013. Primary elections for governor and lieutenant governor were conducted separately on September 9, 2014: the Democrats nominated [[Massachusetts Attorney General]] [[Martha Coakley]] and former CEO of the [[Democratic National Convention]] [[Steve Kerrigan]], and the Republicans nominated former state cabinet secretary and [[2010 Massachusetts gubernatorial election|2010]] gubernatorial nominee [[Charlie Baker]] and former state representative [[Karyn Polito]]. Baker defeated Coakley and three other candidates in the general election. This was the second time in four years that Coakley, despite running as a Democrat in one of the most Democratic-leaning states in the union, lost a statewide election to a Republican. This was her final attempt at winning public office. This election, as of 2026, was the last Massachusetts gubernatorial election where the winning candidate did not both win every county and at least 63% of the vote. ==Democratic primary== ===Governor=== ====Candidates==== * [[Donald Berwick]], former administrator of the [[Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services]] and CEO of the Institute for Healthcare Improvementhttp://www.ihi.org/offerings/IHIOpenSchool/resources/Pages/ProfilesInLeadershipDonBerwick.aspx Profiles in Leadership: Don Berwick{{cite news |last=Murphy |first=Matt |date=June 17, 2013 |title=Berwick Makes Campaign For Governor Official |publisher=WBUR |url=http://www.wbur.org/2013/06/17/berwick-governor-campaign |access-date=June 17, 2013}} * [[Martha Coakley]], [[Massachusetts Attorney General|attorney general of Massachusetts]] and nominee for U.S. Senate [[United States Senate special election in Massachusetts, 2010|in 2010]]{{cite news|last=Phillips|first=Frank|title=Coakley's entry will add to crowded gubernatorial field|url=https://www.bostonglobe.com/metro/2013/09/15/coakley-join-race-for-governor-monday/WSjVtXrvn7mw9ck5MF8k6I/story.html|access-date=September 15, 2013|newspaper=~The Boston Globe|date=September 15, 2013}} * [[Steven Grossman (politician)|Steven Grossman]], [[Treasurer and Receiver-General of Massachusetts|treasurer and receiver-general of Massachusetts]], former chairman of the [[Democratic National Committee]] and [[Massachusetts Democratic Party]]{{cite news | title=Steve Grossman officially announces run for gov. at Mass. Dan Winslow resigns from House, rejoins private sector|date=September 16, 2013|access-date=September 16, 2013|work=[[The Republican (Springfield, Massachusetts)|The Republican]]|first=Shira|last=Schoenberg}} ====Campaign==== At the Republican State Convention on March 22, 2014, Baker received 2,095 votes (82.708%), businessman and Tea Party activist Mark Fisher received 374 votes (14.765%), and there were 64 blank votes (2.527%). The threshold for making the ballot is 15%, and the party announced that Baker had thus received the nomination without the need for a primary election.{{cite news|url=http://boston.cbslocal.com/2014/03/22/mass-gop-expected-to-endorse-governor-senate-candidates-at-convention/|title=Baker Narrowly Avoids Contested GOP Primary For Governor|work=CBS Boston|author=Bob Salsberg|date=March 22, 2014|access-date=April 29, 2014}} However, Fisher argued that according to the convention rules, blank votes are not counted for the purposes of determining the winner, and that he thus received 15.148%, enough to make the ballot. He sued the [[Massachusetts Republican Party|Massachusetts Republican State Committee]], and his case was due to be heard in Suffolk Superior Court between May 2 and June 18.{{cite news|url=http://www.boston.com/politicalintelligence/2014/03/25/mark-fisher-says-will-definitely-sue-state-gop-over-convention-results/Dt7BMJAj1TCYzmoslgx6yL/story.html|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140430060453/http://www.boston.com/politicalintelligence/2014/03/25/mark-fisher-says-will-definitely-sue-state-gop-over-convention-results/Dt7BMJAj1TCYzmoslgx6yL/story.html|url-status=dead|archive-date=April 30, 2014|title=Mark Fisher says he will definitely sue state GOP over convention results|work=The Boston Globe|author=Joshua Miller|date=March 25, 2014|access-date=April 29, 2014}}{{cite news|url=http://www.masslive.com/politics/index.ssf/2014/04/tea_partys_mark_fisher_gets_tr.html|title=Tea Party's Mark Fisher gets trial date in lawsuit against Massachusetts Republican Party over convention vote|work=Mass Live|author=Robert Rizzuto|date=April 24, 2014|access-date=April 29, 2014}} The committee's lawyer, Louis M. Ciavarra, said that in negotiations with the committee, Fisher declined their offer of being placed on the ballot, and instead asked for $1 million in return for dropping the suit. Ciavarra said that after it was pointed out to Fisher and his representatives that this would be illegal, they allegedly lowered their request to $650,000. Fisher's lawyer, Thomas M. Harvey, has confirmed that Fisher had asked for $1 million, which he called a "starting point", saying that Fisher should be "compensated" for his efforts, in addition to receiving a place on the ballot. He later said that the request for $650,000 was "still negotiable" and added that "you don't ask for what you expect".{{cite news|url=http://www.bostonmagazine.com/news/blog/2014/05/07/massgop-cant-get-way/|title=The Massachusetts GOP Can't Get Out of Its Own Way|work=Boston Magazine|author=David S. Bernstein|date=May 7, 2014|access-date=May 8, 2014|archive-date=May 8, 2014|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140508065137/http://www.bostonmagazine.com/news/blog/2014/05/07/massgop-cant-get-way/|url-status=dead}}{{cite news|url=https://www.bostonglobe.com/metro/2014/05/06/gop-fisher-asked-for-million-return-for-dropping-suit/8ntaqeG5Bi5VQcp3vE3HNK/story.html|title=Fisher asked for $1 million to drop lawsuit, GOP says|work=The Boston Globe|author=Frank Phillips|date=May 6, 2014|access-date=May 8, 2014}}{{cite news|url=http://www.bostonmagazine.com/news/blog/2014/05/07/mark-fisher-went-tea-party-crusader-dr-evil/|title=How Mark Fisher Went from Tea Party Crusader to Dr. Evil|work=Boston Magazine|author=Eric Randall|date=May 7, 2014|access-date=May 8, 2014|archive-date=May 8, 2014|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140508222912/http://www.bostonmagazine.com/news/blog/2014/05/07/mark-fisher-went-tea-party-crusader-dr-evil/|url-status=dead}} Fisher himself has denied asking for a "payoff", instead saying that party officials had offered him a "bribe" in December 2013 in return for dropping out. He refused to say who made the offer, claiming to have been under a gag order, though no such order existed.{{cite news|url=http://bostonherald.com/news_opinion/local_politics/2014/05/mark_fisher_fights_for_gop_to_release_docs|title=Mark Fisher fights for GOP to release docs|work=Boston Herald|author=Matt Stout|date=May 9, 2014|access-date=May 12, 2014}}{{cite news|url=https://www.bostonglobe.com/metro/2014/05/11/mark-fisher-ballot-fight-exposes-haplessness-current-day-massachusetts-gop/FGUvTB350BEhTB87Q6UYCN/story.html|title=Fisher's ballot fight exposes GOP haplessness|work=The Boston Globe|author=Adrian Walker|date=May 12, 2014|access-date=May 12, 2014}} He said that he only asked for $1 million during the negotiations because he had been asked for a figure and it was the sum that he claimed the party had offered to him. He further denied the claim that he had offered to withdraw in exchange for the money, saying that he wanted a place on the ballot, for the State Committee to release the "tally sheets" which he claims show that he rightfully won a place on the ballot, and to be reimbursed $100,000 in damages: for the cost of legal fees and of collecting signatures to make the ballot by petition.{{cite news|url=https://www.bostonglobe.com/news/politics/2014/05/08/tea-party-challenger-mark-fisher-calls-rival-charlie-baker-demand-release-documents-convention-vote/IrmvCE7Rxi9bpsPp0ipAeN/story.html|title=GOP candidate demands answers from Charlie Baker, party on dispute|work=The Boston Globe|date=May 8, 2014|access-date=May 12, 2014}} On May 9, 2014, a week into the case, Judge Douglas Wilkins accepted the State Committee's offer to certify Fisher on the primary ballot and put off the expedited June 16 trial date.{{cite news|url=http://www.metrowestdailynews.com/article/20140509/NEWS/140505897/11514/NEWS/?Start=1|title=Republicans relent, will allow Fisher on the primary ballot for governor|work=The Metro West Daily News|author=Matt Murphy|date=May 9, 2014|access-date=May 12, 2014}}{{cite news|url=http://bostonherald.com/news_opinion/us_politics/2014/05/judge_puts_off_trial_as_gop_says_it_will_put_fisher_on_ballot|title=Judge puts off trial as GOP says it will put Fisher on ballot|work=Boston Herald|author=Matt Stout|date=May 9, 2014|access-date=May 12, 2014}} The State Committee had not at that point turned over the "tally sheets" and the judge did not order them to do so, instead inviting Fisher's attorneys to submit an amended complaint. The State Committee also asked that the trial, discovery and deliberation over damages be postponed until after the election. The judge did not rule on that request,{{cite news|url=https://www.bostonglobe.com/metro/2014/05/09/mark-fisher-gop-gubernatorial-primary-ballot-september/QXM8Glj4BXJm3U9XebUB7M/story.html|title=Judge clears way for Fisher to be put on GOP gubernatorial primary ballot|work=The Boston Globe|author=Stephanie Ebbert|date=May 9, 2014|access-date=May 12, 2014}} but he did rule that the other portions of Fisher's complaint would proceed at a later date, with no need for an expedited trial before the primary.{{cite news|url=http://www.telegram.com/article/20140509/NEWS/305099600/1116|title=GOP to clear way for Fisher to appear on primary ballot|work=telegram.com|author=John J. Monahan|date=May 9, 2014|access-date=May 12, 2014}} A debate was held between Baker and Fisher on August 21. They clashed on jobs, gun control and higher education. Baker called for "constructive friction" in electing him governor to counterbalance the Democratic-controlled [[Massachusetts General Court|General Court]] and said that he would "clean up the regulatory morass, control spending [and] reduce taxes." Fisher criticised the rise in food stamps, rising cost of entitlement programmes and illegal immigration.{{cite news|url=http://www.sentinelandenterprise.com/news/ci_26385143/governor-debate-baker-fisher-spar-jobs-gun-control|title=GOVERNOR DEBATE: Baker, Fisher spar on jobs, gun control, higher ed|work=Sentinel & Enterprise|date=August 22, 2014|access-date=September 30, 2015}} In the primary election on September 9, Baker defeated Fisher 116,004 votes (74.1%) to 40,240 (25.7%). In February 2015, Fisher settled with the State Party for $240,000. Executive Director Brian Wynne said that despite the settlement, the Party denied his accusations and said that the settlement was forced on them because of mounting legal costs.{{cite news|url=http://www.wbur.org/2015/02/12/massachusetts-gop-pays-mark-fisher-240000-to-settle-suit|title=Massachusetts GOP Pays Mark Fisher $240,000 To Settle Suit|work=WBUR|date=February 12, 2015|access-date=September 30, 2015}} ====Polling==== {| class="wikitable" |- valign= bottom ! style="width:170px;"| Poll source ! style="width:200px;"| Date(s)

'''Tie:''' {{legend0|#AE8BB1|50%}} | title = [[Governor of Maryland|Governor]] | before_election = [[Martin O'Malley]] | before_party = Democratic Party (United States) | after_election = [[Larry Hogan]] | after_party = Republican Party (United States) }} {{Elections in Maryland sidebar}} The '''2014 Maryland gubernatorial election''' took place on November 4, 2014, to elect the [[Governor of Maryland|governor]] and [[Lieutenant Governor of Maryland|lieutenant governor of Maryland]]. Incumbent [[Democratic Party (United States)|Democratic]] governor [[Martin O'Malley]] was term-limited and could not run for a third consecutive term. Gubernatorial candidates pick their running mates, with the two then running together on the same ticket. Primary elections were held on June 24, 2014. The Democrats nominated incumbent lieutenant governor [[Anthony Brown (Maryland politician)|Anthony Brown]] and [[Howard County, Maryland|Howard County]] [[County executive|Executive]] [[Kenneth Ulman]], while the Republicans nominated former State Secretary of Appointments [[Larry Hogan]], and former State Secretary of General Services and former Assistant U.S. Secretary of Agriculture for Administration [[Boyd Rutherford]]. Brown predicted that winning the general election would be just "a little bit of a molehill",{{cite web|url=https://www.washingtonpost.com/local/md-politics/maryland-governors-race-has-turned-unexpectedly-tight/2014/11/01/7b88147a-60ea-11e4-8b9e-2ccdac31a031_story.html|title=Maryland Governor's race has turned unexpectedly tight|work=The Washington Post|access-date=15 November 2014}} but he lost to Hogan by a margin of 65,510 votes in the [[Politics of Maryland|Democratic-leaning state]].{{cite web|url=http://elections.state.md.us/elections/2014/results/General/gen_results_2014_2_003-.html|title=Unofficial 2014 Gubernatorial General Election results for Governor / Lt. Governor|work=Maryland State Board of Elections|date=November 6, 2014|access-date=November 6, 2014}} ''[[The Washington Post]]'' called the result "a stunning [[upset (competition)|upset]]" and [[Republican Governors Association]] Chair [[Chris Christie]] called it "the biggest upset in the entire country."{{cite news |url=https://www.washingtonpost.com/local/md-politics/republican-larry-hogan-wins-md-governors-race-in-stunning-upset/2014/11/05/9eb8bf46-60ac-11e4-8b9e-2ccdac31a031_story.html?tid=pm_local_pop |title=Republican Larry Hogan wins Md. governor's race in stunning upset |author=John Wagner and Jenna Johnson |date=5 November 2014 |work=The Washington Post}} As of 2026, this is the last Maryland gubernatorial election where the winner received less than 55% of the votes. In 2022, Brown ran successfully for Maryland attorney general after serving in the [[U.S. House of Representatives]] from 2017 to 2023. ==Background== Maryland is considered one of the most Democratic states in the country, and [[Bob Ehrlich]], elected in [[2002 Maryland gubernatorial election|2002]], had been the only Republican elected governor of Maryland since [[Spiro Agnew]] in [[1966 Maryland gubernatorial election|1966]]. Gaztanaga, perennial candidate ===Campaign=== Hogan heavily criticized Brown for his handling of Maryland's health care exchange as a part of the [[Affordable Care Act]], labeling him as "the most incompetent man in Maryland."{{cite web|url=https://www.washingtonpost.com/local/md-politics/a-summer-sequel-hogan-posts-another-ad-on-the-most-incompetent-man-in-maryland/2014/08/05/48a09678-1cd8-11e4-82f9-2cd6fa8da5c4_story.html|title=A summer sequel: Hogan posts another ad on 'the most incompetent man in Maryland'|work=The Washington Post|access-date=15 November 2014}} The Maryland Health Benefit Exchange enrolled fewer than 4,000 people.{{cite web|url=https://www.politico.com/story/2013/12/obamacare-maryland-doug-gansler-101390.html#ixzz3IPDfueMy|title=Obamacare fight erupts in deep-blue Maryland|author=Alexander Burns|work=POLITICO|access-date=15 November 2014}} Hogan avoided social issues by promising not to touch the state's abortion or gun control laws.{{cite web|url=https://www.politico.com/story/2014/11/larry-hogan-maryland-governor-112681_Page2.html#ixzz3IPCBmovq|title=How Larry Hogan won in Maryland|author=Kevin Robillard|work=POLITICO|access-date=15 November 2014}} Campaign ads were a significant part of the first debate, culminating in Hogan's call for Brown to "apologize to the women of Maryland for trying to scare them." Brown pledged no new taxes, no increased taxes, and a look at state spending if elected. Hogan responded by citing O'Malley/Brown's same claim in the 2010 election and how that claim was followed by "40 consecutive tax hikes."{{cite news |url=http://marylandreporter.com/2014/10/07/analyzing-the-gubernatorial-debate-commentators-react/ |title=Analyzing the gubernatorial debate: Commentators react |author=Seven commentators |newspaper=Maryland Reporter |date=October 7, 2014 |access-date=October 25, 2014 |quote=Here are some reactions to last night's debate }} Brown said there have been times he has disagreed with O'Malley, like on mortgage reduction.{{cite news |url=http://baltimore.cbslocal.com/2014/10/07/md-gubernatorial-debate-preview-brown-hogan-face-off/ |title=BLOG: Maryland Gubernatorial Debate Wrap-Up |date=October 7, 2014 |access-date=October 8, 2014 |publisher=WJZ-TV}} "Brown did not stay to take questions from reporters", and both candidates accused the other of not telling the truth.{{cite news |url=https://www.baltimoresun.com/2014/10/07/brown-hogan-accuse-each-other-of-not-telling-truth/ |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20250606165511/https://www.baltimoresun.com/2014/10/07/brown-hogan-accuse-each-other-of-not-telling-truth/ |url-status=live |archive-date=June 6, 2025 |title=Brown, Hogan accuse each other of not telling truth |newspaper=The Baltimore Sun |date=October 7, 2014 |access-date=October 8, 2014 |first1=Michael |last1=Dresser |first2=Erin |url-access=subscription |last2=Cox }} ===Debates=== * [https://www.c-span.org/video/?321969-1/maryland-governors-debate Complete video of debate], October 7, 2014 – [[C-SPAN]] * [https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Gv-G9UF-v-4 Complete video of debate], October 18, 2014 – [[YouTube]] === Predictions === {| class="wikitable" style="text-align:center" |- ! '''Tie:''' {{legend0|#d2b1d9}} | title = Governor | before_election = [[Paul LePage]] | before_party = Republican Party (United States) | after_election = [[Paul LePage]] | after_party = Republican Party (United States) }} {{ElectionsME}} The '''2014 Maine gubernatorial election''' took place on November 4, 2014, to elect the [[governor of Maine]]. Incumbent [[Maine Republican Party|Republican]] Governor [[Paul LePage]] won election to a second term, defeating [[Maine Democratic Party|Democratic]] nominee [[Mike Michaud]], the [[U.S. representative]] from [[Maine's 2nd congressional district]], and [[Independent politician|independent]] [[Eliot Cutler]], an attorney and second-place finisher from the [[2010 Maine gubernatorial election|2010 gubernatorial election]].{{cite web|url=https://bangordailynews.com/slideshow/gov-paul-lepage-wins-a-second-term-2/|title=Gov. Paul LePage wins a second term; Michaud concedes|work=The Bangor Daily News|access-date=November 15, 2014|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20141205015148/http://bangordailynews.com/slideshow/gov-paul-lepage-wins-a-second-term-2/|archive-date=December 5, 2014|url-status=dead|df=mdy-all}} This was one of nine Republican-held governorships up for election in a state that [[Barack Obama]] won in the [[2012 United States presidential election|2012 presidential election]]. This is currently the most recent election that Maine elected a Republican governor. Primary elections were held on June 10, 2014. LePage was initially considered vulnerable in this race, due to persistent approval ratings below 50%. The consensus among ''[[The Cook Political Report]]'',{{cite web|url=http://cookpolitical.com/governor/charts/race-ratings|title=Ratings|access-date=September 6, 2013|archive-date=March 5, 2013|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20130305115607/http://cookpolitical.com/governor/charts/race-ratings|url-status=dead}} ''[[Governing (magazine)|Governing]]''{{cite web |last=Jacobson |first=Louis |url=http://www.governing.com/blogs/politics/gov-handicapping-2013-2014-governors-races-tossups.html |title=Handicapping the 2013–2014 Governors Races: The Tossups |publisher=Governing.com |date=July 18, 2013 |access-date=July 25, 2013 |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20130805052422/http://www.governing.com/blogs/politics/gov-handicapping-2013-2014-governors-races-tossups.html |archive-date=August 5, 2013 |df=mdy-all }} and ''[[Stuart Rothenberg|The Rothenberg Political Report]]''{{cite web|url=http://rothenbergpoliticalreport.com/ratings/governor|title=Ratings|access-date=September 6, 2013}} was that the race was a "tossup" and ''Daily Kos Elections''{{cite web|url=http://www.dailykos.com/story/2013/10/06/1243548/-Daily-Kos-Elections-gubernatorial-race-ratings-Initial-ratings-for-2013-14?detail=hide|title=Daily Kos Elections gubernatorial race ratings: Initial ratings for 2013-14|access-date=November 22, 2013}} and ''[[Sabato's Crystal Ball]]''{{cite web|url=http://www.centerforpolitics.org/crystalball/articles/category/2014-governor/|title=Ratings|access-date=September 6, 2013|archive-date=September 10, 2013|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20130910081704/http://www.centerforpolitics.org/crystalball/articles/category/2014-governor/|url-status=dead}} rated the race as "lean Democratic". On election day, LePage won the election in what was considered a minor upset. As of 2026, this is the last time [[York County, Maine|York]], [[Sagadahoc County, Maine|Sagadahoc]], [[Lincoln County, Maine|Lincoln]], [[Kennebec County, Maine|Kennebec]], [[Waldo County, Maine|Waldo]] and [[Hancock County, Maine|Hancock]] counties did not vote for the Democratic gubernatorial nominee. ==Background== After a close three-way election [[2010 Maine gubernatorial election|in 2010]], Republican [[Paul LePage]], the mayor of [[Waterville, Maine|Waterville]], was elected governor with 38% of the vote. He beat independent candidate Eliot Cutler, who won 36%, and Democrat [[Libby Mitchell]], the [[List of Presidents of the Maine Senate|president]] of the [[Maine Senate]], who won 19%. Republican gubernatorial nominees in Maine have failed to win a majority of the vote in 12 consecutive cycles over the last 50+ years – the longest such GOP streak in the nation.{{cite web |url=http://editions.lib.umn.edu/smartpolitics/2014/03/06/the-elusive-republican-majorit/ |title= The Elusive Republican Majority |work=Smart Politics |first=Eric |last=Ostermeier |date= March 6, 2014}} No governor has been popularly elected with less than 40 percent of the vote in two consecutive cycles in U.S. history.{{cite web |url=http://editions.lib.umn.edu/smartpolitics/2014/10/13/could-paul-lepage-become-the-f/ |title= Could Paul LePage Become the First 30/30 Governor in History? |work=Smart Politics |first=Eric |last=Ostermeier |date= October 13, 2014}} ==Republican primary== ===Candidates=== ====Declared==== * [[Paul LePage]], incumbent governor{{cite web|url=http://www.kjonline.com/politics/Jeb-Bush-supporters-turn-out-for-LePage-re-election-fundraiser.html|title=LePage: I'm running for re-election|publisher=Kennebec Journal|date=July 2, 2013|access-date=July 2, 2013|archive-date=July 5, 2013|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20130705011200/http://www.kjonline.com/politics/Jeb-Bush-supporters-turn-out-for-LePage-re-election-fundraiser.html|url-status=dead}}{{cite web|url=http://www.kjonline.com/politics/With-signatures-LePage-launches-re-election-bid-.html|title=Expanding Medicaid would be 'sinful,' LePage says|publisher=Kennebec Journal |date=March 13, 2014 |access-date=March 14, 2014}} ===Polling=== {{hidden begin|titlestyle=background:#cff|title=Hypothetical polling|contentstyle=border:solid 1px silver; padding:8px; background:var(--background-color-base); color:var(--color-base);}} '''Who should challenge LePage in a primary?'''
