2014 Pennsylvania gubernatorial election.title: 2014 Pennsylvania gubernatorial election
2014 Pennsylvania gubernatorial election.text:
{{Short description|none}} {{Use American English|date=January 2025}} {{Use mdy dates|date=September 2013}} {{Infobox election | election_name = 2014 Pennsylvania gubernatorial election | country = Pennsylvania | type = presidential | ongoing = no | previous_election = 2010 Pennsylvania gubernatorial election | previous_year = 2010 | next_election = 2018 Pennsylvania gubernatorial election | next_year = 2018 | election_date = November 4, 2014 | image_size = 150x150px | image1 = File:Governor Tom Wolf official portrait 2015 (cropped2).jpg | nominee1 = '''[[Tom Wolf]]''' | running_mate1 = '''[[Mike Stack]]''' | party1 = Democratic Party (United States) | popular_vote1 = '''1,920,355 ''' | percentage1 = '''54.93%''' | image2 = File:Governor Corbett cropped portrait May 2014.jpg | nominee2 = [[Tom Corbett]] | running_mate2 = [[Jim Cawley]] | party2 = Republican Party (United States) | popular_vote2 = 1,575,511 | percentage2 = 45.07% | map_image = {{switcher |[[File:2014 Pennsylvania gubernatorial election results map by county.svg|260px]]|County results |[[File:2014 Pennsylvania gubernatorial election results map by congressional district.svg|260px]]|Congressional district results |[[File:2014 PA Governor election by Precinct.svg|260px]] |Precinct results |default=1}} | map_size = 250px | map_caption = '''Wolf:''' {{legend0|#7996e2|50–60%}} {{legend0|#6674de|60–70%}} {{legend0|#584cde|70–80%}} {{legend0|#3933e5|80–90%}} {{legend0|#0E0496|>90%}}
'''Corbett:''' {{legend0|#e27f7f|50–60%}} {{legend0|#d75d5d|60–70%}} {{legend0|#d72f30|70–80%}} {{legend0|#C21B18|80–90%}} {{legend0|#A80000|>90%}}
'''Tie''': {{legend0|#ae8bb1|50%}} {{legend0|#808080|No data}} | title = [[List of Governors of Pennsylvania|Governor]] | before_election = [[Tom Corbett]] | before_party = Republican Party (United States) | after_election = [[Tom Wolf]] | after_party = Democratic Party (United States) | turnout = 36.1%({{decrease}}5.6%) }} {{ElectionsPA}} The '''2014 Pennsylvania gubernatorial election''' was held on November 4, 2014, to elect the [[List of governors of Pennsylvania|governor]] and [[Lieutenant Governor of Pennsylvania|lieutenant governor of Pennsylvania]], concurrently with [[2014 United States Senate elections|elections]] to the [[United States Senate]] in other states and [[2014 United States House of Representatives elections|elections]] to the [[United States House of Representatives]] and various [[2014 United States elections#State elections|state]] and [[2014 United States elections#Local elections|local elections]]. Incumbent Governor [[Tom Corbett]] was defeated by [[Tom Wolf]].{{cite news|title=NBC News Projects: PA's Corbett Ousted by Democrat Tom Wolf|url=http://www.nbcnews.com/politics/elections/nbc-news-projects-pas-corbett-ousted-democrat-tom-wolf-n241396|access-date=November 4, 2014|newspaper=NBC News|date=November 4, 2014}}{{cite news |url=http://articles.philly.com/2014-11-06/news/56395405_1_exit-polls-mount-wolf-democrat-tom-wolf |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20141221005303/http://articles.philly.com/2014-11-06/news/56395405_1_exit-polls-mount-wolf-democrat-tom-wolf |archive-date=2014-12-21 |title=Wolf defeats Corbett |first=Thomas |last=Fitzgerald |date=November 6, 2014 |publisher=philly.com |accessdate=2022-08-03}} This was the only governorship Democrats flipped in the 2014 midterms. Wolf was sworn in on January 20, 2015,{{Cite web |date=2015-01-21 |title=Tom Wolf sworn in as Pennsylvania's 47th governor |url=https://6abc.com/post/tom-wolf-sworn-in-as-pennsylvanias-47th-governor/482762/ |access-date=2025-08-13 |website=6abc Philadelphia |language=en}} marking the most recent time the Pennsylvania governor's office changed partisan control. This was one of nine Republican-held governorships up for election in a state that [[Barack Obama]] won in the [[2012 United States presidential election|2012 presidential election]]. As of 2025, this is the only Pennsylvania gubernatorial election since [[1854 Pennsylvania gubernatorial election|1854]] where the incumbent was defeated,{{efn|In the mid-1800s, governors served three-year terms, and were limited to serving no more than six years of every nine. Beginning with the election of 1874, they were limited to one four-year term. A change to the state constitution in 1968 permitted governors to serve two consecutive four-year terms, then wait at least one term before serving again, with no lifetime limit.}} and the last Pennsylvania gubernatorial election where Cumberland County voted Republican. Dauphin County voted Democratic in a gubernatorial election for the first time since 1990. Corbett was considered vulnerable, as reflected in his low approval ratings. An August 2013 [[Franklin & Marshall College]] poll found that only 17% of voters thought Corbett was doing an "excellent" or "good" job, only 20% thought he deserved to be reelected, and 62% said the state was "off on the wrong track".{{cite web |url=https://edisk.fandm.edu/FLI/keystone/pdf/August%202013%20Franklin%20and%20Marshall%20College%20Poll%20Release.pdf |title=Franklin & Marshall College poll |work=Franklin & Marshall College |date=August 28, 2013 |access-date=November 13, 2013 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20130927221938/https://edisk.fandm.edu/FLI/keystone/pdf/August%202013%20Franklin%20and%20Marshall%20College%20Poll%20Release.pdf |archive-date=September 27, 2013 |url-status=dead |df=mdy-all }} ''[[Politico]]'' called Corbett the most vulnerable incumbent governor in the country,{{cite news|first=Emily|last=Schultheis |title=Pa. Dems line up to run vs. hobbled Corbett|url=https://www.politico.com/story/2013/05/pennsylvania-governor-election-tom-corbett-91277.html|access-date=May 14, 2013|newspaper=PoliticsPA|date=May 13, 2013}} ''[[The Washington Post]]'' ranked the election as the most likely for a party switch,{{cite web|url=http://www.politicspa.com/wapo-pa-gov-1-most-likely-to-switch-parties/49415/|title=WaPo: PA-Gov #1 Most Likely to Switch Parties|date=July 12, 2013|access-date=November 15, 2014}} and the majority of election forecasters rated it "likely Democratic". Wolf in 2014 managed to outperform Barack Obama and Bob Casey Jr.’s performances in the 2012 presidential and U.S. Senate races, respectively. He also won 20 counties that Corbett won in 2010: [[Erie County, Pennsylvania|Erie]], [[Lawrence County, Pennsylvania|Lawrence]], [[Beaver County, Pennsylvania|Beaver]], [[Allegheny County, Pennsylvania|Allegheny]], [[Greene County, Pennsylvania|Greene]], [[Fayette County, Pennsylvania|Fayette]], [[Cambria County, Pennsylvania|Cambria]], [[Centre County, Pennsylvania|Centre]], [[Clinton County, Pennsylvania|Clinton]], [[Northumberland County, Pennsylvania|Northumberland]], [[Dauphin County, Pennsylvania|Dauphin]], [[Luzerne County, Pennsylvania|Luzerne]], [[Monroe County, Pennsylvania|Monroe]], [[Northampton County, Pennsylvania|Northampton]], [[Carbon County, Pennsylvania|Carbon]], [[Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania|Schuylkill]], [[Lehigh County, Pennsylvania|Lehigh]], [[Berks County, Pennsylvania|Berks]], [[Bucks County, Pennsylvania|Bucks]], and [[Chester County, Pennsylvania|Chester]]. Meanwhile, this is the last time these counties have voted Democratic in a statewide election: [[Lawrence County, Pennsylvania|Lawrence]], [[Greene County, Pennsylvania|Greene]], [[Fayette County, Pennsylvania|Fayette]], [[Cambria County, Pennsylvania|Cambria]], [[Clinton County, Pennsylvania|Clinton]], [[Northumberland County, Pennsylvania|Northumberland]], [[Carbon County, Pennsylvania|Carbon]], and [[Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania|Schuylkill]]. This is the first Pennsylvania gubernatorial election since [[1982 Pennsylvania gubernatorial election|1982]] in which the winner was of the same party as the [[Barack Obama|incumbent]] [[President of the United States|president]], and the first time since [[1934 Pennsylvania gubernatorial election|1934]] this occurred during a Democratic administration. This also remains the last time that a Pennsylvania gubernatorial election has been decided by a single-digit margin, as Democrats have won each subsequent election with more than 56% of the vote. 2014 is also the most recent election where Pennsylvania voted for a gubernatorial candidate of a different party from fellow [[Rust Belt]] states Michigan and Wisconsin.{{cite news|url=https://www.cnn.com/2024/09/17/politics/blue-wall-states-harris-trump-analysis/index.html|title=Why these three states are the most consistent tipping point in American politics|publisher=CNN|last=Brownstein|first=Ronald|date=September 16, 2024|accessdate=September 16, 2024}} ==Background== Democrats and Republicans have alternated in the governorship of Pennsylvania every eight years from 1950 to 2010.{{cite book|last=Barone|first=Michael|title=The Almanac of American Politics|year=2014|publisher=University of Chicago Press|location=Chicago|isbn=9780226105444|page=1398}} This has been referred to as "the cycle",{{cite web|last=Madonna|first=Terry|title=The Eight-Year Cycle - Believe It!|url=http://www.fandm.edu/politics/politically-uncorrected-column/2009-politically-uncorrected/the-eight-year-cycle-believe-it|publisher=Franklin & Marshall College|access-date=January 28, 2014|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140201193402/http://www.fandm.edu/politics/politically-uncorrected-column/2009-politically-uncorrected/the-eight-year-cycle-believe-it|archive-date=February 1, 2014|url-status=dead}}{{cite book|last=Baer|first=John M.|title=On the Front Lines of Pennsylvania Politics|year=2012|publisher=The History Press|location=Charleston|isbn=9781609497156|page=71}} but it was broken with a Democratic Party win in 2014. Pennsylvania has also voted against the party of the sitting president in 18 of the last 19 gubernatorial contests dating back to 1938; Democrats lost 16 of the previous 17 Pennsylvania gubernatorial races with a Democratic president in the White House, a pattern begun in 1860.{{cite web |url=http://editions.lib.umn.edu/smartpolitics/2013/08/26/pennsylvania-democrats-hope-to/ |title= Pennsylvania Democrats Hope to Reverse History in 2014 Gubernatorial Race |work=Smart Politics |first=Eric |last=Ostermeier |date= August 26, 2013}} The last incumbent governor to be defeated for re-election was Democrat [[William Bigler]] in [[1854 Pennsylvania gubernatorial election|1854]]. Until 1968, governors could only serve one term; the state constitution now allows governors to serve two consecutive terms.Pennsylvania Constitution article IV, § 3. Libertarian nominee Ken Krawchuk failed to file the paperwork to be on the ballot in time and was excluded from the election as a result. ==Republican primary== Incumbent [[Tom Corbett]] filed to run, as did [[Bob Guzzardi]], an attorney and conservative activist. However, Guzzardi failed to file a statement of financial interests as required by law, after being told by an employee of the State Department that it was unnecessary. Four Republicans, backed by the state Republican Party, sued to have him removed from the race. The case reached the state Supreme Court, which ordered that Guzzardi's name be struck from the ballot.{{cite news | url=http://www.delcotimes.com/government-and-politics/20140501/corbetts-gop-foe-bob-guzzardi-ordered-off-pa-primary-ballot | title=Corbett's GOP foe Bob Guzzardi ordered off Pa. primary ballot | work=The Delaware County Daily Times | date=1 May 2014 | access-date=21 May 2014 | author=Jackson, Peter}} [[NASCAR]] [[Camping World Truck Series]] veteran [[Norm Benning]] backed Governor Corbett during the later half of the NASCAR season with "Re-Elect Tom Corbett" posted on his truck. ===Candidates=== ====Declared==== * [[Tom Corbett]], incumbent governor of Pennsylvania ====Disqualified==== * [[Bob Guzzardi]], attorney, businessman and conservative activist{{cite news|url=http://www.politicspa.com/conservative-activist-mounts-primary-challenge-to-corbett/53515/|title=Conservative Activist Mounts Primary Challenge to Corbett|newspaper=PoliticsPA|first=Keegan|last=Gibson|date=December 10, 2013|access-date=December 14, 2013}}{{cite news|url=http://www.politicspa.com/supreme-court-strikes-guzzardi-from-pa-gov-ballot/57458/|title=Supreme Court Strikes Guzzardi From PA-Gov Ballot|newspaper=PoliticsPA|author=Brittany Foster|date=May 1, 2014|access-date=May 5, 2014}} ====Declined==== * [[Bruce Castor]], [[Montgomery County, Pennsylvania|Montgomery County]] Commissioner{{cite news|first=Keegan|last=Gibson|title=Breaking: Castor Rules Out 2014 Run|url=http://www.politicspa.com/breaking-castor-rules-out-2014-run/47849/|access-date=May 7, 2013|newspaper=PoliticsPA|date=May 8, 2013}} * [[Jim Gerlach]], U.S. Representative and candidate for governor [[2010 Pennsylvania gubernatorial election|in 2010]]{{cite news|url=http://www.politicspa.com/breaking-rep-gerlach-will-not-seek-reelection/53983/|title=Breaking: Rep. '''Tie:''' {{legend0|#efe7f5|}} {{legend0|#808080|No votes}} | title = [[List of governors of Rhode Island|Governor]] | before_election = [[Lincoln Chafee]] | before_party = Democratic Party (United States) | after_election = [[Gina Raimondo]] | after_party = Democratic Party (United States) }} {{ElectionsRI}} The '''2014 Rhode Island gubernatorial election''' took place on November 4, 2014, to elect the [[List of governors of Rhode Island|governor of Rhode Island]], concurrently with [[2014 United States Senate election in Rhode Island|the election]] of Rhode Island's [[Classes of United States senators|Class II U.S. Senate seat]], as well as [[2014 United States Senate elections|other elections]] to the United States Senate in other states and [[2014 United States House of Representatives elections|elections]] to the [[United States House of Representatives]] and various [[2014 United States elections#State elections|state]] and [[2014 United States elections#Local elections|local elections]]. Incumbent [[Democratic Party (United States)|Democratic]] governor [[Lincoln Chafee]] was eligible to run for re-election to a second term but decided to retire. He had been elected as an [[independent candidate]] and became a Democrat in 2013.{{Cite web |title=Gov. Chafee Officially Joins Democratic Party {{!}} Campaign 2014 {{!}} WPRI.com |url=http://wpri.com/dpp/news/local_news/mcgowan/warwick-ri-gov-lincoln-chafee-officially-becomes-democrat |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20130609054220/http://wpri.com/dpp/news/local_news/mcgowan/warwick-ri-gov-lincoln-chafee-officially-becomes-democrat |archive-date=2013-06-09 |access-date=2026-04-24 |website=WPRI TV |language=en-US}} In primary elections held on September 9, 2014, the Democrats nominated [[State treasurer|Rhode Island Treasurer]] [[Gina Raimondo]] and the Republicans nominated [[Cranston, Rhode Island|Cranston]] Mayor [[Allan Fung]]. Also on the ballot were [[Robert J. Healey]] of the [[Moderate Party of Rhode Island|Moderate Party]] and two [[Independent politician|Independent]] candidates. Raimondo won the election, becoming the first Democrat to be elected governor since [[Bruce Sundlun]] in [[1992 Rhode Island gubernatorial election|1992]], as Chafee had been elected as an independent [[2010 Rhode Island gubernatorial election|in 2010]]. Raimondo became the first female governor in Rhode Island history. Democrats won Newport County for the first time in a gubernatorial election since [[1998 Rhode Island gubernatorial election|1998]], and Bristol and Washington counties since [[1992 Rhode Island gubernatorial election|1992]]. ==Background== In the [[2010 Rhode Island gubernatorial election|2010 gubernatorial election]], Republican incumbent [[Donald Carcieri]] was term-limited and unable to seek a third term in office. The Republicans nominated businessman John Robitaille and the Democrats nominated State Treasurer [[Frank T. Caprio]]. Also contesting the election were [[Moderate Party of Rhode Island|Moderate Party]] nominee [[Ken Block (politician)|Ken Block]] and [[Lincoln Chafee]], who served as a Republican U.S. senator from 1999 to 2007. After losing a bid for re-election [[2006 United States Senate election in Rhode Island|in 2006]], Chafee left the Republican Party and became an independent, running for governor as such. After a close three-way race between Chafee, Robitaille and Caprio, Chafee won the election with a plurality, taking 36% to Robitaille's 34%, Caprio's 23% and Block's 6%. After constant speculation during his term, Chafee officially joined the Democratic Party on May 30, 2013. He had previously indicated that he might run for re-election as an independent or a Democrat.{{cite web|url=http://www.boston.com/news/local/rhode-island/2012/12/14/gov-chafee-open-running-for-term-dem/Q5g9thzMcZzorBrTmyOYuM/story.html|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20130910052032/http://www.boston.com/news/local/rhode-island/2012/12/14/gov-chafee-open-running-for-term-dem/Q5g9thzMcZzorBrTmyOYuM/story.html|url-status=dead|archive-date=September 10, 2013|title=RI Gov. Chafee open to running for 2nd term as Dem|date=December 14, 2012|access-date=December 18, 2012|agency=[[Associated Press]]|publisher=[[Boston.com]]|first=David|last=Klepper}} In the face of low approval ratings, polling showing him trailing in both the Democratic primary and the general election, and with weak fundraising, Chafee announced on September 4, 2013, that he would not run for re-election.{{cite news|url=https://www.washingtonpost.com/blogs/the-fix/wp/2013/09/04/why-lincoln-chafees-decision-not-to-run-for-reelection-is-more-good-news-for-democrats/|title=Why Lincoln Chafee's decision not to run for reelection is more good news for Democrats|date=September 4, 2013|access-date=September 6, 2013|newspaper=The Washington Post|first=Sean|last=Sullivan}}{{cite web|url=http://firstread.nbcnews.com/_news/2013/09/04/20327881-gov-chafee-wont-run-for-a-second-term?lite|title=Gov. Chafee won't run for a second term|date=September 4, 2013|access-date=September 6, 2013|work=NBC News|first=Jessica|last=Taylor}} Chafee thus became just the fourth governor in the history of Rhode Island to decline to seek a second term, after [[Byron Diman]] in 1847, [[Royal C. Taft]] in 1889 and [[William S. Flynn]] in 1924.{{cite web|url=http://blog.lib.umn.edu/cspg/smartpolitics/2013/09/chafee_just_4th_rhode_island_g.php|title=Chafee Just 4th Rhode Island Governor Since 1790 to Pass On 2nd Term|date=September 6, 2013|access-date=September 6, 2013|work=Smart Politics|first=Eric|last=Ostermeier|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20131004070640/http://blog.lib.umn.edu/cspg/smartpolitics/2013/09/chafee_just_4th_rhode_island_g.php|archive-date=October 4, 2013|url-status=dead}} ==Democratic primary== Gina Raimondo, Treasurer of Rhode Island, and Angel Taveras, mayor of Providence, announced their campaigns in late 2013 and the race initially seemed to be between the more fiscally moderate Raimondo and the more progressive Taveras. However, the entry of Clay Pell, an Obama administration official and grandson of [[Claiborne Pell]], into the race complicated things. Unions who had criticized Raimondo for cutting pension benefits and investing in hedge funds during her tenure as Treasurer and for fundraising from Wall Street and national lobbyists were split on whether to back Taveras or Pell. A coalition of unions including firefighters, police, supermarket clerks, and city employees backed Taveras, whereas the powerful teachers' unions backed Pell, unimpressed with Taveras' support for [[charter school]]s. Raimondo drew support from non-union and private sector workers and some private sector unions including iron workers. Pell spent over $3.4 million of his own money and ran a positive campaign, but he was much criticized for his inexperience and lack of ties to Rhode Island. Taveras emphasised his background as the son of poor Dominican immigrants to appeal to Latino and working-class voters. All three candidates agreed not to seek the endorsement of the state Democratic Party. Ultimately, Taveras and Pell took an almost equal share of the vote as progressive Democrats split their vote between the two, allowing Raimondo to win with a plurality. Raimondo won 36 of the state's 39 municipalities. Taveras won [[Central Falls, Rhode Island|Central Falls]] and Pell won [[Burrillville, Rhode Island|Burrillville]] and [[Foster, Rhode Island|Foster]].{{cite '''Sheheen''': {{legend0|#a5b0ff|40–50%}} {{legend0|#7996e2|50–60%}} {{legend0|#6674de|60–70%}} {{legend0|#584cde|70–80%}} | title = [[Governor of South Carolina|Governor]] | before_election = [[Nikki Haley]] | before_party = Republican Party (United States) | after_election = [[Nikki Haley]] | after_party = Republican Party (United States) }} {{ElectionsSC}} The '''2014 South Carolina gubernatorial election''' took place on November 4, 2014, to elect the [[governor of South Carolina]], concurrently with the [[United States Senate election in South Carolina, 2014|regularly-scheduled election]] and [[United States Senate special election in South Carolina, 2014|special election]] to both of South Carolina's [[Classes of United States senators|U.S. Senate seats]], as well as [[2014 United States Senate elections|other elections]] to the United States Senate in other states and [[2014 United States House of Representatives elections|elections]] to the [[United States House of Representatives]] and various [[2014 United States elections#State elections|state]] and [[2014 United States elections#Local elections|local elections]]. Incumbent [[Republican Party (United States)|Republican]] Governor [[Nikki Haley]] ran for a second term in office. She faced [[Democratic Party (United States)|Democratic]] State Senator [[Vincent Sheheen]] in the general election. Republican-turned-independent [[Tom Ervin]] had been running, but he withdrew from the race and endorsed Sheheen. Haley defeated Sheheen for the second time, winning with nearly 56 percent of the vote.{{Cite web |url=http://www.thestate.com/2014/11/09/3801867/democratic-nominee-for-2018-its.html |title = Democratic nominee for 2018? '''Tie:''' {{legend0|#d2b1d9|40–50%}} | title = [[Governor of South Dakota|Governor]] | before_election = [[Dennis Daugaard]] | before_party = Republican Party (United States) | after_election = [[Dennis Daugaard]] | after_party = Republican Party (United States) }} {{ElectionsSD}} The '''2014 South Dakota gubernatorial election''' took place on November 4, 2014, to elect the [[Governor of South Dakota|governor]] and [[lieutenant governor of South Dakota]], concurrently with the [[United States Senate election in South Dakota, 2014|election]] of South Dakota's [[Classes of United States senators|Class II U.S. Senate seat]], as well as other elections to the [[2014 United States Senate elections|United States Senate]] in other states, elections to the [[2014 United States House of Representatives elections|United States House of Representatives]], and various state and local elections. Incumbent [[Republican Party (United States)|Republican]] governor [[Dennis Daugaard]] ran for re-election to a second term in office. He won the Republican primary and ran again with incumbent lieutenant governor [[Matt Michels]]. The [[Democratic Party (United States)|Democrats]] nominated State Representative [[Susan Wismer]], who chose former state representative [[Susy Blake]] as her running mate. [[Independent politician|Independent]] Mike Myers also ran, whose running mate was former Republican state representative [[Lora Hubbel]]. ==Republican primary== ===Candidates=== ====Declared==== * Bill Haslam Visit to ETTP 2014 Oak Ridge (cropped) (cropped).jpg }}{{ElectionsTN}} The '''2014 Tennessee gubernatorial election''' took place on November 4, 2014, to elect the [[governor of Tennessee]], alongside other state and [[2014 Tennessee elections|local elections]]. [[Incumbent]] [[Republican Party (United States)|Republican]] governor [[Bill Haslam]] was re-elected to a second term with 70.3% of the vote, defeating his [[Democratic Party (United States)|Democratic]] challenger Charles Brown. Improving on his performance from [[2010 Tennessee gubernatorial election|2010]], Haslam also carried every county in the state.{{Cite web |title=2014 Gubernatorial General Election Results - Tennessee |url=https://uselectionatlas.org/RESULTS/state.php?year=2014&fips=47&off=5&elect=0&f=0 |access-date=2026-03-08 |website=uselectionatlas.org}} It was the largest margin of victory for any candidate in the [[2014 United States gubernatorial elections|2014 gubernatorial elections.]] The [[Partisan primary|primary elections]] took place on August 7, 2014, with [[Republican Party (United States)|Republican]] [[Bill Haslam]] and Democrat Charles Brown winning their respective party nominations. With no political experience, Charles Brown campaigned on raising speed limits on the interstate highways to [[Miles per hour|80 mph]] and putting the [[Bible]] back in schools.{{Cite web |last=Murphy |first=Tim |title=Tennessee gubernatorial nominee explains why he wants to electrocute governor |url=https://www.motherjones.com/politics/2014/08/charlie-brown-bill-haslam-tennessee/ |access-date=2024-06-10 |website=Mother Jones |language=en-US}} Some of the [[Tennessee Democratic Party]] members became concerned over Brown's candidacy when he said in an interview that he would like to put Bill Haslam in an electric chair and "turn it on about half throttle and let him smell a little bit."{{Cite AV media |url=https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=OlgGfzTXr7g |title=Charlie Brown running for Tennessee governor. Good grief! |date=2014-08-12 |last=chattanooga times free press |access-date=2024-06-10 |via=YouTube}}{{Cite web |date=2014-08-08 |title=Dem Gubernatorial Nominee Wants To Send Governor To Electric Chair |url=https://www.huffpost.com/entry/charlie-brown-bill-haslam-tennessee_n_5662940 |access-date=2024-06-10 |website=HuffPost |language=en}}{{Cite news |last=Hannan |first=Caleb |date=2014-08-08 |title=The Alvin Greene of 2014 |url=https://slate.com/news-and-politics/2014/08/charlie-brown-democratic-candidate-for-tennessee-governor-the-72-year-old-hunter-who-did-no-campaigning.html |access-date=2024-06-10 |work=Slate |language=en-US |issn=1091-2339}} Haslam, on the other hand, campaigned on jobs, economic development, education reform, workforce development, and conservative fiscal leadership.{{Cite web |date=2021-06-11 |title=Priorities |url=https://www.tn.gov/former-governor-haslam/priorities.html |access-date=2024-06-10 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210611195727/https://www.tn.gov/former-governor-haslam/priorities.html |archive-date=June 11, 2021 }}{{Cite web |date=2014-10-21 |title=Bill Haslam's Accomplishments |url=http://www.billhaslam.com/accomplishments/ |access-date=2024-06-10 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20141021011451/http://www.billhaslam.com/accomplishments/ |archive-date=October 21, 2014 }} As of {{CURRENTYEAR}}, this was the best performance in a Tennessee gubernatorial election since [[Buford Ellington]]'s victory in [[1966 Tennessee gubernatorial election|1966]]. '''Tie:''' {{legend0|#d2b1d9|40–50%}} {{legend0|#ae8bb1|50%}} {{legend0|#808080|No data}} | title = [[Governor of Texas|Governor]] | before_election = [[Rick Perry]] | before_party = Republican Party (United States) | after_election = [[Greg Abbott]] | after_party = Republican Party (United States) }} {{Elections in Texas sidebar}} The '''2014 Texas gubernatorial election''' was held on November 4, 2014, to elect the [[governor of Texas]]. Incumbent [[Republican Party (United States)|Republican]] governor [[Rick Perry]], who had served since the resignation of then-Governor [[George W. Bush]] on December 21, 2000, declined to run for an unprecedented fourth full term, making this the first [[open seat|open election]] for governor of the state since [[1990 Texas gubernatorial election|1990]]. The election took place between nominees who were selected on March 4, 2014: Republican [[Texas Attorney General|State Attorney General]] [[Greg Abbott]] and Democratic [[Texas Senate|State Senator]] [[Wendy Davis (politician)|Wendy Davis]]. Also on the ballot were [[Libertarian Party (United States)|Libertarian Party]] candidate Kathie Glass{{cite web | url=https://www.lptexas.org/texas-statewide-offices/84-candidates/1118-2014-statewide-offices-list | title=2014 Statewide Offices List | publisher=Libertarian Party of Texas | access-date=July 15, 2014 | archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140726081410/https://www.lptexas.org/texas-statewide-offices/84-candidates/1118-2014-statewide-offices-list | archive-date=July 26, 2014 | url-status=dead }} and [[Green Party (United States)|Green Party]] candidate Brandon Parmer.{{cite web|url=http://web.txgreens.org/|title=Green Party of Texas - Peace * Justice * Democracy * Ecology|access-date=October 11, 2014}} Abbott was projected to carry the election, and ultimately won handily with a 20.4 percentage point advantage.{{cite web|url=http://www.chron.com/news/houston-texas/houston/article/Polls-open-for-the-midterm-election-5868589.php|title=Up and down the ballot, a night of dominance for GOP in Texas and in Harris County|work=Houston Chronicle|date=November 5, 2014 |access-date=November 15, 2014}} As of 2022, this is the most recent gubernatorial election in which [[Bexar County, Texas|Bexar]], [[Harris County, Texas|Harris]] and [[Hays County, Texas|Hays]] counties voted Republican. Exit polls showed Abbott winning Whites (72% to 25%), while Davis received majorities among African Americans (92% to 7%) and Hispanics (55% to 44%). Abbott won roughly half of Hispanic men, 54% of all women, and 62% of married women.{{cite web|url=http://www.foxnews.com/politics/elections/2014/exit-polls?year=2014&type=governor&filter=TX|title=2014 Exit Polls - Politics - Fox News|work=Fox News|access-date=November 15, 2014}} Abbott 2014 Vermont gubernatorial election.text:

'''Milne:''' {{legend0|#FFB2B2|40–50%}} {{legend0|#E27F7F|50–60%}} {{legend0|#D75D5D|60–70%}} {{legend0|#D72F30|70–80%}} {{legend0|#C21B18|80–90%}}
'''Tie:''' {{legend0|#d2b1d9|40–50%}} {{legend0|#808080|No votes}} | title = [[Governor of Vermont|Governor]] | before_election = [[Peter Shumlin]] | before_party = Democratic Party (United States) | after_election = [[Peter Shumlin]] | after_party = Democratic Party (United States) }} {{ElectionsVT}} The '''2014 Vermont gubernatorial election''' took place on November 4, 2014, to elect the [[List of governors of Vermont|governor of Vermont]], concurrently with [[2014 United States Senate elections|elections]] to the [[United States Senate]] in other states, [[2014 United States House of Representatives elections|elections]] to the [[United States House of Representatives]], and various [[2014 United States elections#State elections|state]] and [[2014 United States elections#Local elections|local elections]]. Incumbent [[Democratic Party (United States)|Democratic]] governor [[Peter Shumlin]] ran for reelection to a third term in office against [[Republican Party (United States)|Republican]] businessman [[Scott Milne]], [[Libertarian Party (United States)|Libertarian]] businessman Dan Feliciano and several other minor party and independent candidates. Based on election polling, Shumlin's large financial advantage and the state's [[Red states and blue states|strong Democratic lean in presidential elections]], Shumlin was expected to win easily, but he received only a [[Plurality (voting)|plurality]], not a [[majority]], of the vote and polled only 2,434 votes more than Milne out of 193,087 cast. The [[Constitution of Vermont]] requires that the 180-member [[Vermont General Assembly]] choose the winner when no candidate receives over 50% of the popular vote.{{cite news|title=Close election recalls recent recounts|url=http://www.burlingtonfreepress.com/story/news/politics/2014/11/06/election-recalls-recent-recounts/18622085/|access-date=November 11, 2014|work=The Burlington Free Press|date=November 7, 2014}} As a result, on January 8, 2015,{{cite news|url=http://vtdigger.org/2014/12/08/video-scott-milne-asks-lawmakers-vote-january/|title=Trail Mix: Milne concedes he won't concede|work=VTDigger|author=Anne Galloway|date=December 8, 2014|access-date=January 4, 2015}} the Assembly chose Shumlin over Milne by a vote of 110 to 69, with one abstention.{{cite news|url=http://www.burlingtonfreepress.com/story/news/politics/2015/01/08/vermont-legislature-vote/21394309/|title=Shumlin defeats Milne in Legislature governor vote|author=Free Press Staff|date=January 8, 2015|access-date=January 8, 2015}} The result of the election prompted much debate and analysis amongst commentators and the political parties. The [[2014 United States elections|2014 U.S. elections]] saw Republicans make sweeping gains in federal, state, and local offices across the country, and Republicans won gubernatorial victories in the Democratic-leaning Northeastern states of [[2014 Maryland gubernatorial election|Maryland]] and [[2014 Massachusetts gubernatorial election|Massachusetts]]. With a margin of 1.3%, this election was the second-closest race of the [[2014 United States gubernatorial elections|2014 gubernatorial election cycle]], behind only [[2014 Florida gubernatorial election|the election in Florida]]. {{As of|2026}}, this was also the last time a Democrat won the governorship of Vermont. ==Background== Four-term Republican governor [[Jim Douglas]] did not run for reelection [[2010 Vermont gubernatorial election|in 2010]]. In the race to succeed him, Democratic nominee [[Peter Shumlin]], the [[President pro tempore of the Vermont State Senate|president pro tempore]] of the [[Vermont Senate]], received 49.5% of the vote while Republican nominee [[List of lieutenant governors of Vermont|Lieutenant Governor]] [[Brian Dubie]] received 47.7%. As neither candidate received a majority, the General Assembly was required to pick the winner in January 2011. Dubie did not contest the vote; he conceded the race on election night and called for Vermont to "unite" around Shumlin.{{cite web |url=http://www.vpr.net/news_detail/89189/dubie-asks-vermonters-to-unite-around-new-governor/ |title=Dubie Asks Vermonters To Unite Around New Governor |work=Vermont Public Radio |date=November 3, 2010 |access-date=August 3, 2013}} Shumlin won the Assembly vote 145 to 28, with seven legislators not voting.{{cite web|url=http://www.burlingtonfreepress.com/article/20101103/NEWS02/101103024/1007/news02/Dubie-concedes-to-Shumlin-in-Vermont-governor-a-race|title=Dubie concedes to Shumlin in Vermont governor race|publisher=burlingtonfreepress.com|date=2010-11-03}}{{Dead link|date=July 2018 |bot=InternetArchiveBot |fix-attempted=yes }}Vermont General Assembly, [http://www.leg.state.vt.us/docs/2012/journal/ja110106.pdf Journal of the Joint Assembly], January 6, 2011, page 5 Shumlin was reelected [[2012 Vermont gubernatorial election|in 2012]] against Republican state senator and former [[Vermont Auditor of Accounts]] [[Randy Brock]] by a landslide, 57.8% to 37.6%.{{cite web|url=http://www.ourcampaigns.com/RaceDetail.html?RaceID=726426|title=VT Governor 2014|publisher=Our Campaigns|access-date=February 28, 2016}} Vermont and [[New Hampshire]] are the only states in the country whose governors are elected every two years. An incumbent governor of Vermont had not been defeated for reelection since [[1962 Vermont gubernatorial election|1962]], when Democrat [[Philip H. Hoff]] beat Republican [[F. Ray Keyser, Jr.]] by 1,315 votes.{{cite web |url=http://www.ourcampaigns.com/ContainerHistory.html?ContainerID=282 |title=VT Governor 1962 |access-date=August 3, 2013}} ==Democratic primary== Shumlin announced in December 2013 that he was running for reelection to a third term in office, but said that he would not begin campaigning until after [[Labor Day (United States)|Labor Day]] 2014, just two months before the election.{{cite web|url=http://www.7dvt.com/2013cashing-shumlin-dials-dollars-he-seeks-third-term|title=Cashing In: Shumlin Dials for Dollars as He Seeks a Third Term|date=December 4, 2013|access-date=December 9, 2013|work=Seven Days}} He faced one opponent in the Democratic primary on August 26: lifelong Republican and Washington, D.C. resident [[H. Brooke Paige]],{{cite web |url=http://www.ourcampaigns.com/RaceDetail.html?RaceID=807715 |title=VT Governor - D Primary 2014 |access-date=February 28, 2016}} who simultaneously ran against Democratic incumbent [[William Sorrell]] in the [[2014 Vermont elections#Attorney General|Democratic primary election]] for [[Vermont attorney general]]. Paige was also unsuccessful in that effort, losing by 80% to 20%.{{cite web |url=http://www.ourcampaigns.com/RaceDetail.html?RaceID=807718 |title=VT Attorney General - D Primary 2014 |access-date=February 28, 2016}} ===Candidates=== ====Nominee==== * [[Peter Shumlin]], incumbent governor ==== Eliminated in primary ==== * [[H. Brooke Paige]], former CEO of Remington News Service and Republican candidate for the U.S. Senate [[United States Senate election in Vermont, 2012|in 2012]] ([[2014 Vermont elections#Attorney General|''also ran for attorney general'']]){{cite web|url=http://rutlandherald.com/article/20140614/NEWS03/706149920|title=Paige begins two-pronged political battle|date=June 14, 2014|access-date=November 14, 2014|work=Rutland Herald|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20141124161103/http://rutlandherald.com/article/20140614/NEWS03/706149920|archive-date=November 24, 2014|url-status=dead|df=mdy-all}}{{cite web|url=http://www.burlingtonfreepress.com/story/news/politics/2014/06/16/modern-day-mark-twain-joins-governor-race/10628751/|title=Modern-day Mark Twain joins governor race|date=June 19, 2014|access-date=November 14, 2014|work=Seven Days}}{{cite news|url=https://www.washingtonpost.com/blogs/the-fix/wp/2014/08/26/where-can-you-run-for-two-offices-at-once-vermont-of-course/|title=Where can you run for two offices at once? Vermont, of course.|date=August 26, 2014|access-date=November 14, 2014|newspaper=The Washington Post}} ===Results=== {{Election box begin no change | title = Democratic primary results{{cite web|url=http://az357346.vo.msecnd.net/resultsSW.aspx?type=SW&map=MPRC |title=Unofficial Results - Primary Election - August 26, 2014 |access-date=September 28, 2014 |publisher=Vermont Secretary of State |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140903042919/http://az357346.vo.msecnd.net/resultsSW.aspx?type=SW&map=MPRC |archive-date=September 3, 2014 }} }} {{Election box winning candidate with party link no change | candidate = [[Peter Shumlin]] (incumbent) | party = Democratic Party (United States) | votes = 15,260 | percentage = 76.96% }} {{Election box candidate with party link no change | candidate = [[H. Brooke Paige]] | party = Democratic Party (United States) | votes = 3,199 | percentage = 16.13% }} {{Election box candidate with party link no change | candidate = Write-in | party = Democratic Party (United States) | votes = 1,369 | percentage = 6.9% }} {{Election box total no change | votes = 19,828 | percentage = 100% }} {{Election box end}} ==Republican primary== The Republicans initially struggled to recruit a candidate. Former governor Douglas and [[List of lieutenant governors of Vermont|Lieutenant Governor]] [[Phil Scott]] announced early on that they would not run, and it was not until March 2014 that a candidate entered the race: marijuana legalization activist and former Independent gubernatorial candidate Emily Peyton.{{cite web|url=http://blogs.burlingtonfreepress.com/politics/2014/03/07/theres-a-candidate-running-for-governor-as-a-republican-but-isnt-really-from-the-party/|title=There's a candidate running for governor as a Republican — but isn't really from the party|date=March 7, 2014|access-date=March 13, 2014|work=The Burlington Free Press|author=Nancy Remsen}} This spurred Republicans to recruit a serious candidate, but they struggled to do so. Former [[Wall Street]] banker Bruce Lisman announced in May 2014 that he was not running, and attention turned to former state senator and 2012 nominee [[Randy Brock]], State Representative [[Heidi Scheuermann]] and businessman [[Scott Milne]].{{cite web|url=http://www.burlingtonfreepress.com/story/news/local/2014/05/12/republican-milne-considers-run-governor/9009379/|title=Republican Milne considers run for governor|date=May 12, 2014|access-date=May 13, 2014|work=The Burlington Free Press|author=Terri Hallenbeck}} In May, Scheuermann said that she would not run, leaving the party with a month until the June 12 filing deadline to find a candidate.{{cite web|url=http://www.burlingtonfreepress.com/story/news/local/2014/05/13/scheuermann-opts-run-governor/9032953/|title=Scheuermann opts against run for governor|date=May 13, 2014|access-date=May 13, 2014|work=The Burlington Free Press|author=Terri Hallenbeck}} Milne, who was traveling in Africa, announced that he would decide shortly before the deadline. Brock was urged to run and considered doing so,{{cite web|url=http://www.wptz.com/news/vermont-new-york/burlington/brock-decision-on-2014-run-for-governor-imminent/26255234|title=Brock decision on 2014 run for governor imminent|date=May 30, 2014|access-date=November 18, 2014|work=WPTZ|author=Stewart Ledbetter}} but revealed on June 8 that he would not.{{cite web|last1=Brown|first1=Tom|title=Brock bows out of GOP race for governor, Milne 'on the fence'|url=http://vtdigger.org/2014/06/08/brock-bows-gop-race-governor-milne-fence/|work=VTDigger|date=June 8, 2014 |access-date=June 9, 2014}} On the morning of filing deadline day, Milne announced that he would run.{{cite web|author=Peter Hirschfeld|title=Republican Scott Milne Looks To Unseat Peter Shumlin|url=http://digital.vpr.net/post/republican-scott-milne-looks-unseat-peter-shumlin|website=VPR.net|date=June 12, 2014 |publisher=Vermont Public Radio|access-date=June 20, 2014}} He was joined in the Republican primary by Peyton and retired marketer and self-described "modern-day [[Mark Twain]]" Steve Berry. Also running but not appearing on the ballot was Dan Feliciano, who ran as a write-in candidate for the Republican nomination and was uncontested for the Libertarian nomination.{{cite web|url=http://www.burlingtonfreepress.com/story/news/politics/2014/08/23/vermont-gop-governor-primary/14462577/|title=GOP to choose a governor candidate|work=The Burlington Free Press|date=August 23, 2014|access-date=August 24, 2014|first=Terri|last=Hallenbeck}} In the August 26 primary, Milne was nominated with over 70% of the vote.{{cite web |url=http://www.ourcampaigns.com/RaceDetail.html?RaceID=807716 |title=VT Governor - R Primary 2014 |access-date=February 28, 2016}} ===Candidates=== ====Nominee==== * [[Scott Milne]], businessman, candidate for the state house in 2006 and son of former state legislators [[Donald Milne|Don]] and [[Marion Milne]] ==== Eliminated in primary ==== * Steve Berry, retired marketer{{cite web |author=Kyle Midura |date=June 12, 2014 |title=GOP challenger to take on Gov. Shumlin won 112, or 40.7%, and they were tied in one other.{{cite news|last1=Heintz|first1=Paul|title=Close Call: Seven Reasons Shumlin Nearly Lost|url=http://www.sevendaysvt.com/vermont/close-call-seven-reasons-shumlin-nearly-lost/Content?oid=2472138|access-date=November 13, 2014|work=Seven Days|date=November 12, 2014}} Shumlin won the state's biggest voting area, [[Burlington, Vermont|Burlington]] (representing 9,604 gubernatorial voters), by a margin of 66% to 23%. Of the state's 10 largest municipalities, Shumlin also won [[South Burlington, Vermont|South Burlington]], [[Bennington, Vermont|Bennington]], [[Montpelier, Vermont|Montpelier]], [[Hartford, Vermont|Hartford]] and [[Middlebury, Vermont|Middlebury]]. Milne won [[Essex, Vermont|Essex]], [[Colchester, Vermont|Colchester]], [[Rutland (city), Vermont|Rutland City]], [[Williston, Vermont|Williston]] and [[Barre (town), Vermont|Barre Town]]. Of Vermont's 13 multi-member Senate districts, aligning roughly with the state's 14 counties, Milne won eight (61.5%) and Shumlin five (38.5%). Milne won the popular vote in 53 House districts; Shumlin won in 51. ==General Assembly vote== Since 1853, the General Assembly has selected the first-place finisher in every gubernatorial election that has come before it,{{cite news|url=http://www.timesargus.com/article/20141110/NEWS03/711109999 |title=Plurality or politics? |date=November 10, 2014 |access-date=November 11, 2014 |work=Barre Montpelier Times Argus}} most recently in [[2010 Vermont gubernatorial election|2010]], when Shumlin received 49.5% of the vote and was chosen over Republican Brian Dubie, and in [[2002 Vermont gubernatorial election|2002]], when the Democratic-controlled legislature picked Republican [[Jim Douglas]], who had received 44.9%, over Democrat [[Doug Racine]], who received 42.4%.{{cite news|url=http://vtdigger.org/2014/11/10/lawmakers-likely-stick-secret-ballot/ |title=Lawmakers likely to stick with secret ballot |date=November 10, 2014 |access-date=November 11, 2014 |work=VT Digger}} The Assembly most recently reversed a plurality vote in the 1976 lieutenant gubernatorial election, when the Republican-controlled legislature picked Republican [[T. Garry Buckley]] rather than Democrat John Alden, who was suspected, and later convicted, of insurance fraud.{{cite news|title=Close election recalls recent recounts|url=http://www.burlingtonfreepress.com/story/news/politics/2014/11/06/election-recalls-recent-recounts/18622085/|access-date=November 13, 2014|work=The Burlington Free Press|date=November 7, 2014}}{{cite news|title=T. Garry Buckley|url=http://www.timesargus.com/apps/pbcs.dll/article?AID=/20120527/FEATURES15/705279943/1014/OPINION06|access-date=November 13, 2014|work=Barre Montpelier Times Argus|date=May 27, 2012|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20141113162135/http://www.timesargus.com/apps/pbcs.dll/article?AID=%2F20120527%2FFEATURES15%2F705279943%2F1014%2FOPINION06|archive-date=November 13, 2014|url-status=dead|df=mdy-all}}{{cite news|url=http://digital.vpr.net/post/wait-legislature-choosing-governor|title=Wait, The Legislature Is Choosing The Governor?|access-date=November 13, 2014|publisher=Vermont Public Radio|date=November 6, 2014}} Although the second-place finisher usually concedes the race, as happened in 2002 and 2010,{{cite news|url=http://edition.cnn.com/2002/ALLPOLITICS/11/06/elec02.governor/index.html|archive-url=https://archive.today/20141113155328/http://edition.cnn.com/2002/ALLPOLITICS/11/06/elec02.governor/index.html|url-status=dead|archive-date=November 13, 2014|title=Two candidates claim Alabama gubernatorial race|date=November 7, 2002|access-date=November 13, 2014|publisher=CNN}}{{cite news|url=http://www.huffingtonpost.com/2010/11/03/vermont-election-results-_2_n_773154.html|title=Vermont Election Results: Brian Dubie Concedes To Peter Shumlin In 2010 Governor's Race|date=November 3, 2010|access-date=November 13, 2014|work=The Huffington Post}} Milne refused to concede. He considered requesting a recount, but did not do so, reasoning that it was "extremely unlikely, almost unfathomable, that a recount would put either candidate above the 50 percent mark."{{cite news|url=http://wamc.org/post/milne-wont-seek-recount-may-ask-legislators-elect-him-governor|title=Milne Won't Seek Recount, But May Ask Legislators To Elect Him Governor|access-date=November 14, 2014|publisher=WAMC|date=November 13, 2014|archive-date=November 29, 2014|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20141129021839/http://wamc.org/post/milne-wont-seek-recount-may-ask-legislators-elect-him-governor|url-status=dead}} Before the election, Milne said that if Shumlin won a plurality, he would support him and would expect Shumlin to do the same if the situation were reversed. After the election, however, he said, "it's clear that 54% of Vermonters want a new governor, and a new path forward."{{cite news|url=http://www.rutlandherald.com/article/20141106/THISJUSTIN/141109966|title=Milne Calls Shumlin's Claim of Victory Premature|access-date=November 7, 2014|work=Rutland Herald|date=November 6, 2014}} As 91 votes are needed to elect the governor from the 180-member body and Democrats and Progressives held 112 seats, it was considered unlikely that Milne would win.{{cite news|url=http://vtdigger.org/2014/11/12/scott-milne-pursuit-governorship/ |title=Margolis: Scott Milne and the pursuit of the governorship |work=VT Digger |date=November 12, 2014 |access-date=November 23, 2014}} Milne argued that legislators should decide the election in line with how their individual districts voted.{{cite news|author=Laura Krantz|title=Milne exploring all options|url=http://vtdigger.org/2014/11/06/milne-exploring-options/|access-date=November 13, 2014|work=VTDigger|date=November 6, 2014}} Neal Goswami of the Vermont Press Bureau calculated that if each legislator voted according to the results in their district, the vote would result in a 90–90 tie. Milne disagreed with this calculation and claimed voting according to district outcome would result in his winning 93–87. {{quote box |width = 29em |border = 1px |align = right |halign = left |quote = ''The fact is that fewer people voted for Scott Milne than voted for Peter Shumlin. Milne did not get a majority, either. I just don't think he has a case to be made that a majority, or even a plurality of voters, want him to be governor. I don't think that I will probably have to persuade [other legislators of this], quite frankly.'' |source = [[Speaker of the Vermont House of Representatives|State House Speaker]] [[Shap Smith]], whose district voted for Milne, explaining why he would vote for Shumlin }} Republican legislative leaders said that they would not [[Whip (politics)|whip]] their members to vote for Shumlin, leaving them free to vote their consciences. Though Republican [[Lieutenant Governor of Vermont|lieutenant governor]] [[Phil Scott]] did not have a vote, he said that he would vote for Shumlin, and Republican state representative [[Kurt Wright]] said that he would do so.{{cite news |url=http://www.berkshireeagle.com/news/ci_26895237/vermont-gop-says-party-will-follow-conscience-governor |title=Vermont: GOP says party will follow conscience on governor vote |work=The Berkshire Eagle |date=November 8, 2014 |access-date=November 11, 2014 |archive-date=November 12, 2014 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20141112001928/http://www.berkshireeagle.com/news/ci_26895237/vermont-gop-says-party-will-follow-conscience-governor |url-status=dead }} Initially, no Democrats indicated that they would vote for Milne. Indeed, several Democrats whose districts voted for Milne over Shumlin said that they would vote for Shumlin, citing his plurality win. For almost a month, Milne made no further comment as he considered whether to lobby for legislators' votes.{{cite news |url=http://www.mychamplainvalley.com/story/d/story/republican-scott-milne-asks-legislature-to-vote-fo/31865/0LSmLUglskiTLbU9p21mGQ |title=Republican Scott Milne Asks Legislature to Vote For Him |work=My Champlain Valley |author1=Steph Machado |author2=Lesley Engle |date=December 8, 2014 |access-date=January 4, 2014 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150104162128/http://www.mychamplainvalley.com/story/d/story/republican-scott-milne-asks-legislature-to-vote-fo/31865/0LSmLUglskiTLbU9p21mGQ |archive-date=January 4, 2015 |url-status=dead |df=mdy-all }}{{cite news|url=http://vtdigger.org/2014/11/12/milne-may-drop-recount-likely-wont-concede/ |title=Milne may drop recount, likely won't concede |work=VTDigger |author=Laura Krantz |date=November 12, 2014 |access-date=January 4, 2014}}{{cite news|url=http://www.greenmountaindaily.com/diary/10752/milne-mulls-his-next-move |title=Milne mulls his next move |work=Green Mountain Daily |author=Laura Krantz |date=November 12, 2014 |access-date=January 4, 2014}} Former governor Douglas cautioned Milne against waging a legislative campaign for governor, saying that it was "unlikely" to be an effective strategy and that Milne should seek to preserve the "good will that he has accrued" and "acknowledge the result and come back and fight another day."{{cite news|url=http://digital.vpr.net/post/douglas-milne-dont-wage-legislative-campaign-governor |title=Douglas To Milne: Don't Wage Legislative Campaign For Governor |publisher=Vermont Public Radio |author=Bob Kinzel |date=November 10, 2014 |access-date=January 4, 2014}} [[File:Jim Douglas-2009.jpg|left|thumb|225px|Former Republican Governor Jim Douglas, who urged Milne not to campaign for votes in the General Assembly]] On December 8, Milne held a press conference in which he defied suggestions that he would concede by officially announcing that he was asking state legislators to vote for him. He went on to say that he would not be "pro-actively" trying to convince legislators to vote for him, nor would he start "twisting arms", but that his "door is open" and called on legislators to "consider the record of the incumbent" and what was "best" for Vermont.{{cite news|url=http://www.burlingtonfreepress.com/story/news/politics/2014/12/08/milne-announces-plan-seek-election/20088821/ |title=Milne continues push for governor's office |work=Burlington Free Press |author=April Burbank |date=December 8, 2014 |access-date=January 4, 2014}}{{cite news|url=http://www.montpelierbridge.com/2014/12/scott-milne-up-close-and-personal-qa/ |title=Scott Milne: Up Close and Personal Q&A |work=The Bridge |date=December 19, 2014 |access-date=January 4, 2014}} Shumlin responded that he was "honored to have received the most votes in this election and would not want to serve as governor if I did not." He went on to say that he believed that "the Legislature will honor the long democratic tradition of electing the candidate who received the most votes." After Milne's announcement, Independent State Representative Paul Poirier, a liberal whose district voted for Milne by a 2-to-1 margin, announced that he would vote for Milne. One Democrat, State Representative Jim Condon, said that he would vote for Milne, also citing his district's support for Milne over Shumlin. Political science professors Eric Davis and Garrison Nelson and House Minority Leader Don Turner expected the General Assembly vote to roughly follow party lines, with Milne receiving about one-third of the votes, including most of the Republicans and a few Democrats and Independents. On December 17, Shumlin announced that he was dropping his plan to implement single-payer healthcare. The reforms, which required business and personal tax increases, had never advanced beyond the framework stage. Shumlin, who had missed two earlier financing deadlines, said that "this is not the right time" because the federal government had offered less funding than expected and "the potential economic disruption and risks would be too great to small businesses, working families and the state's economy."{{cite news|url=https://www.politico.com/story/2014/12/vermont-peter-shumlin-single-payer-health-care-113653.html |title=Vermont bails on single-payer health care |work=Politico |author=Sarah Wheaton |date=December 17, 2014 |access-date=January 4, 2014}} The media also cited controversy surrounding comments made by economist [[Jonathan Gruber (economist)|Jonathan Gruber]], who was involved in crafting and advocating for the plan, and Shumlin's failure to win a majority in the election as reasons for the cancellation.{{cite web |url=https://www.bloomberg.com/politics/articles/2014-12-18/how-math-lawsuits-and-jonathan-gruber-killed-vermonts-singlepayer-health-care-dream |title=How Math, Lawsuits, and Jonathan Gruber Killed Vermont's Single-Payer Health Care Dream |author=David Weigel |work=Bloomberg | date=December 18, 2014 |access-date=January 4, 2015}} The decision, which Shumlin called the "biggest disappointment" of his career, drew a mixed response.{{cite web |url=http://www.vnews.com/home/14858908-95/decision-draws-mixed-response |title=Shumlin's Single-Payer Decision Draws Mixed Response |author=Rick Jurgens |work=Valley News |date=December 18, 2014 |access-date=January 4, 2015}}{{cite news |url=http://www.timesargus.com/article/20141219/NEWS03/712199989 |title=Some emboldened, others enraged by demise of single payer |work=Barre Montpelier Times Argus |date=December 19, 2014 |access-date=January 4, 2014 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150104200035/http://www.timesargus.com/article/20141219/NEWS03/712199989 |archive-date=January 4, 2015 |url-status=dead |df=mdy-all }} Business groups lauded his "pragmatic" move but supporters of health care reform organized protests and said that it would end his political career.{{cite web |url=http://vtdigger.org/2015/01/01/year-review-health-care-drama-unfolds/ |title=Year in review: health care drama unfolds |author=Morgan True |work=VTDigger |date=January 1, 2015 |access-date=January 4, 2015}}{{cite web |url=http://vtdigger.org/2014/12/18/protesters-demand-action-single-payer-condemn-shumlins-betrayal/ |title=Protesters demand action on single pater, condemn Shumlin's reversal |author=Morgan True |work=VTDigger |date=December 18, 2014 |access-date=January 4, 2015}} At the end of December, the newly formed group "Vermonters for Honest Government" raised $30,000 to air television advertisements aimed at pressuring legislators to vote for Milne. The group's founder, retired [[United States Navy]] Captain Bill Round, said that legislators should vote against Shumlin because "he's promised a lot and failed to deliver."{{cite news|url=https://vtdigger.org/2014/12/30/group-launches-ad-grassroots-effort-pressure-lawmakers-vote-milne/ |title=Group launches ad, grassroots effort to pressure lawmakers to vote for Milne |work=VTDigger |author=Anne Galloway |date=December 30, 2014 |access-date=January 4, 2014}}{{cite news |url=http://wamc.org/post/group-running-ads-urging-legislature-vote-milne-governor |title=Group Running Ads Urging Legislature To Vote For Milne For Governor |publisher=Vermont Public Radio |author=Pat Bradley |date=December 30, 2014 |access-date=January 4, 2014 |archive-date=January 4, 2015 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150104181711/http://wamc.org/post/group-running-ads-urging-legislature-vote-milne-governor |url-status=dead }} Round did not reveal the source of the group's funding. Milne said that while he had no connection to the group, he appreciated the sentiment.{{cite news|url=http://digital.vpr.net/post/group-runs-ad-calling-election-scott-milne |title=Group Runs Ad Calling For Election Of Scott Milne |publisher=Vermont Public Radio |author=Peter Hirschfeld |date=December 30, 2014 |access-date=January 4, 2014}} By contrast, Shumlin said that he would "absolutely not" run any advertisements, nor would he campaign for legislators' votes or spend any money. He added that he was "not worried" about the vote.{{cite news|url=http://www.burlingtonfreepress.com/story/news/politics/2014/12/30/shumlin-says-worried-vote/21056955/ |title=Shumlin says he's not worried about vote |publisher=Burlington Free Press |author=Peter Hirschfeld |date=December 31, 2014 |access-date=January 6, 2014}} In early January, Milne reiterated that he was not actively campaigning for legislators' votes but said that he felt that his odds of victory were "getting better on a weekly basis, if not a daily basis."{{cite news|url=http://www.burlingtonfreepress.com/story/news/local/2015/01/03/milne-says-odds-improving/21231247/ |title=Milne says his odds improving |work=Burlington Free Press |author=Dave Gram |date=January 3, 2014 |access-date=January 4, 2014}} Shumlin said that if Milne were to win, Vermont would be "paralyzed", as the new administration lacked the time needed to assemble a new staff and draft a budget for the 2016 fiscal year. He also offered his support for amending the state constitution so that as long as a plurality winner received at least 40% of the vote, the Assembly would not be required to decide the election.{{cite news|url=http://www.burlingtonfreepress.com/story/news/politics/2015/01/05/milne-shumlin-vermont-governor-legislature/21300367/ |title=Lawmakers to decide gubernatorial election Thursday |work=Burlington Free Press |author=Dave Gram |date=January 6, 2014 |access-date=January 8, 2014}} On January 8, the General Assembly voted to reelect Shumlin by 110 votes to 69, with one legislator not voting. Shumlin stated that he was "grateful for the opportunity to continue serving this state I love. I expect this will be a productive session addressing the issues Vermonters care about so deeply." Milne said that it was "a good day for Vermont ... I was happy to be a part of it. I think the road that's led us here has a lot of people feeling like one person can make a difference." Milne did not rule out running again [[2016 Vermont gubernatorial election|in 2016]], although he later declined and instead [[2016 United States Senate election in Vermont|ran for the United States Senate]], losing to incumbent [[Patrick Leahy]] by almost 30 points.{{cite news|url=https://www.politico.com/story/2015/01/peter-shumlin-scott-milne-vermont-governor-race-114051.html |title=Vermont legislature to pick next governor Thursday |work=Politico |author=Kyle Cheney |date=January 7, 2014 |access-date=January 8, 2014}} ===Results=== {{Election box begin no change | title = 2014 Vermont gubernatorial election, Vermont General Assembly vote}} {{Election box winning candidate with party link no change | party = Democratic Party (United States) | candidate = [[Peter Shumlin]] (incumbent) | votes = 110 | percentage = 61.45% }} {{Election box candidate with party link no change | party = Republican Party (United States) | candidate = [[Scott Milne]] | votes = 69 | percentage = 38.55% }} {{Election box candidate with party link no change| |party = Libertarian Party (United States) |candidate = Dan Feliciano |votes = 0 |percentage = 0.00% }} {{Election box total no change | votes = 179 of 180 | percentage = 100.00% | change = }} {{Election box hold with party link without swing |winner = Democratic Party (United States) }} {{Election box end}} ==Analysis== As no candidate received a majority of the vote, the [[Vermont General Assembly]] was required to decide the election, choosing among the top three vote-getters, Shumlin, Milne and Feliciano. The result came as a surprise to most observers, who had expected Shumlin to win easily.{{cite news|url=http://www.wptz.com/news/vermont-new-york/burlington/people-react-to-vermont-governors-race/29571318 |title=People react to Vermont governor's race |publisher=WPTZ |date=November 5, 2014 |access-date=November 13, 2014}}{{cite news|url=http://www.stowetoday.com/stowe_reporter/news/article_46a6096a-653b-11e4-a88b-f3f03141b952.html |title=Milne nearly topples Shumlin |work=Stowe Reporter |date=November 5, 2014 |access-date=November 13, 2014}}{{cite news|url=http://www.thedailybeast.com/articles/2014/11/13/what-the-hell-happened-in-vermont.html |title=What the Hell Happened in Vermont?! |work=The Daily Beast |date=November 13, 2014 |access-date=November 13, 2014}} [[RealClearPolitics]] rated the race "Likely Democratic" and ''[[The Cook Political Report]]'', ''[[Daily Kos|Daily Kos Elections]]'', ''[[Governing (magazine)|Governing]]'', ''[[Stuart Rothenberg|The Rothenberg Political Report]]'' and ''[[Sabato's Crystal Ball]]'' all rated the race "Safe Democratic".[[2014 United States gubernatorial elections#Safe seats]] RealClearPolitics reported an average lead in the polls of 15.2% for Shumlin{{cite news|url=http://www.realclearpolitics.com/epolls/2014/governor/vt/vermont_governor_milne_vs_shumlin-5207.html |title=Vermont Governor - Milne vs. Shumlin |work=RealClearPolitics |access-date=November 11, 2014}} and HuffPost Pollster's model estimated Shumlin would beat Milne 51.1% to 37% with the probability that Shumlin would win the election at 95%.{{cite news |url=http://elections.huffingtonpost.com/pollster/2014-vermont-governor-milne-vs-shumlin |title=2014 Vermont Governor: Milne vs. Shumlin |work=elections.huffingtonpost.com |date=October 27, 2014 |access-date=November 11, 2014 |archive-date=November 11, 2014 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20141111192510/http://elections.huffingtonpost.com/pollster/2014-vermont-governor-milne-vs-shumlin |url-status=dead }} [[File:Leahy2009.jpg|right|thumb|225px|Democratic U.S. Senator Patrick Leahy, whose support Shumlin touted]] Analyzing the results, ''[[The Burlington Free Press]]'' pointed to Shumlin's relatively soft numbers in opinion polls – he was in the mid-40s in the last four polls of the race – as evidence that voters were dissatisfied with the progress the state had made in instituting [[Vermont health care reform|single-payer health care]], with rising property taxes, and with the unsuccessful roll-out of [[Vermont Health Connect]], the state's [[Health insurance marketplace|federal health care exchange]].{{cite news|url=http://www.burlingtonfreepress.com/story/news/politics/2014/11/05/two-term-incumbent-governor-nearly-lost/18563053/ |title=How a two-term incumbent governor nearly lost |work=The Burlington Free Press |date=November 6, 2014 |access-date=November 11, 2014}} Shumlin's internal polls showed a close race and he touted an endorsement from U.S. senator [[Patrick Leahy]] to try to put him over 50%. By comparison, Milne lagged in fundraising and spending, with $100,000 available compared to Shumlin's $1.1 million, which meant that he could not afford to pay for polling. Opinions varied about the effect Libertarian nominee Dan Feliciano's candidacy had on the result. Former governor [[Jim Douglas|Douglas]] suggested that Feliciano split the anti-Shumlin vote. ''The Burlington Free Press'' speculated that Feliciano drew voters dissatisfied with Shumlin but who would have voted for Milne if they had realized that he had a chance to prevail. Feliciano stated that he was "not a spoiler" but drew voters who could not bring themselves to vote for the Republican candidate. A Feliciano campaign consultant felt, based on polling, that her candidate's stance against Shumlin's healthcare policy garnered votes. Milne, who did no polling, began criticizing Shumlin's healthcare policy later in the campaign than Feliciano. Republicans wondered whether they should have done more to push Feliciano out, whether Milne should have run more strongly against single-payer, whether 2012 nominee and former state auditor [[Randy Brock]] should have run again, and whether the state party should have been less focused on state legislative races. Analysis by political experts pointed to the record-low voter turnout–around 43.6%–and that 39,000 more people voted for Democratic congressman [[Peter Welch]] than voted for Shumlin as a sign of dissatisfaction with Shumlin. [[University of Vermont]] political science professor Garrison Nelson said that "the people who showed up are the angry ones" and that, unlike Shumlin, "Welch demonstrated an appeal far beyond just the Democratic base."{{cite news|url=http://vtdigger.org/2014/11/11/analysis-many-voters-stayed-home-rather-back-shumlin/ |title=Analysis: many voters stayed home rather than back Shumlin |work=VT Digger |date=November 11, 2014 |access-date=November 18, 2014}} In a news conference on November 12, Shumlin stated that the result was "humbling" and said that he would "listen, learn, reflect [and] be more inclusive." He also pledged to move ahead with single-payer health care and to address school spending, property taxes and the $100-million budget gap.{{cite news|url=http://vtdigger.org/2014/11/12/humbled-shumlin-vows-listen-learn/ |title=Shumlin committed to single-payer, vows to listen, learn |work=VT Digger |date=November 12, 2014 |access-date=November 18, 2014}} On June 8, 2015, Shumlin announced that he would not run for a fourth term in [[2016 Vermont gubernatorial election|2016]]. He said that he had "never seen politics as a lifelong career" and "decided to make this decision now because I want these next 18 months to be about the work that we still have to do." He said that his decision was "not driven by poll numbers; [nor] driven by politics" and that after leaving office in January 2017, he would return to his family business in [[Putney, Vermont|Putney]].{{cite news|url=http://www.burlingtonfreepress.com/story/news/2015/06/08/shumlin-decided-against-2016-re-election/28690591/ |title=Shumlin decides against 2016 re-election bid |work=Burlington Free Press |date=June 8, 2015 |access-date=June 8, 2015}} Several candidates announced their intention to run: for the Democrats, former state senator and [[2010 Vermont gubernatorial election|2010]] gubernatorial candidate [[Matt Dunne]],{{cite web|url=http://www.burlingtonfreepress.com/story/news/politics/2015/09/02/dunne-announces-run-governor/71571840/|title=Dunne announces run for governor|work=[[The Burlington Free Press]]|author=Paris Achen|date=September 2, 2015|access-date=October 1, 2015}} former secretary of the [[Vermont Agency of Transportation]] and former state representative [[Sue Minter]]{{cite web|url=http://www.sevendaysvt.com/OffMessage/archives/2015/09/10/sue-minter-to-run-for-vermont-governor|title=Sue Minter to Run for Vermont Governor|work=[[Seven Days (newspaper)|Seven Days]]|author=Terri Hallenbeck|date=September 10, 2015|access-date=September 20, 2015}} and [[Speaker of the Vermont House of Representatives|Speaker]] of the [[Vermont House of Representatives]] [[Shap Smith]];{{cite web|url=http://www.burlingtonfreepress.com/story/news/politics/2015/08/22/shap-smith-speaker-questions/32157113/|title=Analysis: Should Shap step down as speaker?|work=Burlington Free Press|author=Paris Achen|date=August 22, 2015|access-date=August 22, 2015}} for the Republicans, retired banker Bruce Lisman{{cite web|url=http://vtdigger.org/2015/09/01/lisman-makes-2016-republican-gubernatorial-bid-official/|title=Lisman makes 2016 Republican gubernatorial bid official|work=VTDigger.org|author=Morgan True|date=September 1, 2015|access-date=September 1, 2015}} and Lieutenant Governor [[Phil Scott]].{{cite web|url=http://www.sevendaysvt.com/OffMessage/archives/2015/09/08/scott-pins-gubernatorial-campaign-on-fiscal-responsibility|title=Scott Pins Gubernatorial Campaign on 'Fiscal Responsibility'|work=sevendaysvt.com|author=Terri Hallenbeck|date=September 8, 2015|access-date=September 8, 2015}} Milne did not run again. Milne later clarified that he expected Scott to win the nomination and, in September 2015, officially endorsed him.{{cite web|url=http://www.sevendaysvt.com/OffMessage/archives/2015/09/29/scott-milne-backs-phil-scott-for-governor|title=Scott Milne Backs Phil Scott for Governor|work=[[Seven Days (newspaper)|Seven Days]]|author=Terri Hallenbeck|date=September 29, 2015|access-date=October 1, 2015}} Libertarian nominee Dan Feliciano, who joined the Republican Party in mid-January 2015,{{cite '''Burke:''' {{legend0|#7996e2|50–60%}} {{legend0|#6674de|60–70%}} {{legend0|#584cde|70–80%}} | title = [[Governor of Wisconsin|Governor]] | before_election = [[Scott Walker (politician)|Scott Walker]] | before_party = Republican Party (United States) | after_election = [[Scott Walker (politician)|Scott Walker]] | after_party = Republican Party (United States) |turnout=54.5% ({{decrease}} 3.3%)}} {{ElectionsWI}} The '''2014 Wisconsin gubernatorial election''' took place on November 4, 2014, to determine the [[Governor of Wisconsin|governor]] and [[Lieutenant Governor of Wisconsin|lieutenant governor]] of the [[U.S. state]] of [[Wisconsin]]. It occurred concurrently with [[2014 United States Senate elections|elections]] to the [[United States Senate]] in other states, [[2014 United States House of Representatives elections|elections]] to the [[United States House of Representatives]], and various [[2014 United States elections#State elections|state]] and [[2014 United States elections#Local elections|local elections]]. This was one of nine Republican-held governorships up for election in a state that [[Barack Obama]] won in the [[2012 United States presidential election|2012 presidential election]]. Incumbent [[Republican Party (United States)|Republican]] governor [[Scott Walker (politician)|Scott Walker]] won re-election to a second term in office, defeating [[Democratic Party (United States)|Democratic]] businesswoman and [[Madison Metropolitan School District|Madison school board]] member [[Mary Burke]] and two minor party candidates in the general election. Walker, who was elected [[2010 Wisconsin gubernatorial election|in 2010]], survived an attempted recall [[2012 Wisconsin gubernatorial recall election|in 2012]], the first governor in United States history to do so, defeating Democrat [[Tom Barrett (Wisconsin politician)|Tom Barrett]] both times. Wisconsin voters had elected a governor from a different political party than the sitting president in 27 of the last 31 elections since 1932; only once has a Democratic candidate been elected governor in Wisconsin in the last 18 contests when a Democrat was in the White House.{{cite web |url=http://editions.lib.umn.edu/smartpolitics/2013/08/23/scott-walkers-ticket-to-ride-o/ |title= Scott Walker's Ticket to Ride: Obama in the White House? |work=Smart Politics |first=Eric |last=Ostermeier |date= August 23, 2013}} Eleven of the last twelve Wisconsin governors, dating back to Republican [[Vernon Wallace Thomson]] in the late 1950s, had, unlike Burke, previously won an election to state government, the exception being Republican [[Lee S. Dreyfus]] in 1978.{{cite web |url=http://editions.lib.umn.edu/smartpolitics/2014/09/17/wisconsin-gubernatorial-pathwa/ |title= Wisconsin Gubernatorial Pathways: How Does Burke's Measure Up? |work=Smart Politics |first=Eric |last=Ostermeier |date= September 17, 2014}} The polling leading up to the election was very close, with no candidate clearly in the lead. The consensus among most analysts was that the race was either a tossup or leaning Republican. '''Gosar:''' {{legend0|#a5b0ff|40–50%}} | title = [[Governor of Wyoming|Governor]] | before_election = [[Matt Mead]] | before_party = Republican Party (United States) | after_election = [[Matt Mead]] | after_party = Republican Party (United States) }} {{ElectionsWY}} The '''2014 Wyoming gubernatorial election''' was held on November 4, 2014, to elect the [[List of governors of Wyoming|governor of Wyoming]]. The election coincided with elections to other federal and state offices. Incumbent [[Republican Party (United States)|Republican]] governor [[Matt Mead]] ran for re-election to a second term in office. Mead won the election with 59% of the vote, defeating [[Democratic Party (United States)|Democrat]] Pete Gosar, [[Independent (politician)|Independent]] candidate Don Wills and [[Libertarian Party (United States)|Libertarian]] Dee Cozzens. ==Republican primary== ===Candidates=== ====Declared==== * Taylor Haynes, physician, rancher and Independent write-in candidate for governor [[2010 Wyoming gubernatorial election|in 2010]]{{cite web|url=http://kgab.com/haynes-announces-run-for-governor/|title=Haynes Announces Run For Governor|date=April 29, 2013|access-date=January 20, 2014|work=KGAB.com|author=Doug Randall}} * Cindy Hill, State Superintendent of Public Instruction{{cite web|url=http://kgab.com/hill-announces-run-for-governor-in-2014/|title=Hill Announces Run for Governor in 2014|date=January 31, 2013|access-date=January 20, 2014|work=KGAB.com|author=Doug Randall}} * [[Matt Mead]], incumbent governor{{cite web|url=http://meadforgovernor.com/governor-matt-mead-announces-2014-re-election-campaign|title=Governor Matt Mead Announces 2014 Re-Election Campaign|date=March 11, 2014|access-date=March 12, 2014|work=meadforgovernor.com|author=Kari Gray|archive-date=March 13, 2014|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140313044828/http://meadforgovernor.com/governor-matt-mead-announces-2014-re-election-campaign/|url-status=dead}} ===Polling=== {| class="wikitable" |- valign= bottom ! style="width:145px;"| Poll source ! style="width:160px;"| Date(s)
